title: America’s Latest Inflation Check-In Doesn’t Look Good for Trump
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
America just had its last major checkup on inflation ahead of the midterm elections, and the results aren’t looking good

Yesterday, the Bureau of Labor Statistics released September’s update to the Consumer Price Index, one of the most important metrics for understanding how much Americans actually pay for goods and services. (Among them: cupcakes, dental care, sports equipment.) Overall, costs for consumers have been rising faster than economists expected
They’re up 3.7 percent over the past year, and September marked the largest monthly increase since April—much of which had to do with massive Iran-war-driven spikes in energy prices
That’s just the first half of the problem
At the same time, the BLS revealed yesterday that Americans now have less spending power than they did earlier this year
Real wages—the average amount, adjusted for inflation, that workers earn an hour—have tumbled back down to about where they were when Donald Trump retook the presidency last January
Prices are now rising so fast, across so many different industries, that they’ve overwritten nearly two years of wage gains
As the economist Jared Bernstein put it in his CPI postmortem today, “It’s one thing to cope with high prices when your earnings are at least keeping pace with inflation

But when they’re falling behind … well, that makes for a much tougher equation.” Kevin Hassett, the Trump-appointed director of the National Economic Council, said yesterday that he sees a “whole bunch of good news” in the CPI report—namely food prices (they’ve held relatively steady) and prescription-drug prices, which have gotten lower (something he credits to Trump’s online drugstore )
The sheer scope of the data makes it easy to cherry-pick examples
The prices of both milk and cookies have gone down since August too, so at least Trump’s economy has been good to Santa
But as economists and Democratic politicians have been quick to point out, the overwhelming majority of the data don’t support that optimism
For example, the prices of other everyday goods, such as coffee, clothing, and hardware, have all gone up
Taken together, the BLS numbers offer a compelling explanation for Americans’ frustrations with the cost of living

Another recent report helps put those frustrations in context: People’s confidence in the economy is approaching a record low, per the preliminary October results of the University of Michigan’s consumer-sentiment survey
And according to today’s BLS data on wholesale prices, businesses are reckoning with higher costs too
The Producer Price Index is now at its highest level in four years
The price spikes are the result of a “perfect storm” of macroeconomic forces, Heather Long, the chief economist at the Navy Federal Credit Union, told me
The AI boom , for example, is clearly behind some of September’s computer-related increases
Bernstein told me over email that the breadth of last month’s price movement is part of what’s so concerning
Even when you strip away the volatile energy and food categories, what’s known as the “core” inflation rate is still up 2.6 percent year-over-year
Widespread hikes across these core categories—including housing, hotels, and recreational goods—suggest that the problem has to do with more than just foreign policy
Still, these new BLS reports carry dire warnings for the president and his party
When Trump began his second term, he claimed to have inherited the worst inflation in United States history

Today, inflation is rising faster than it was last January, and Trump’s own actions have undercut his claim that we’re living through an economic “Golden Age.” The tariffs that he implemented last year had a dramatic impact on all kinds of consumer goods

Without those duties, economists at the New York Fed estimate that prices would have declined into early 2026. “For every percentage point increase in average tariffs, consumer goods prices increase by about a quarter of a percent,” the report reads
The president’s decision to bring the country into a costly, protracted war with Iran has also made energy more expensive around the world
In America, gasoline alone is up 9.1 percent since last month and up 34.2 percent since last September, per the BLS
Trying to reclaim the narrative, Trump has recently been putting some of the blame on Ukraine

He said on Saturday that President Volodymyr Zelensky “wants to make problems for the world” by attacking Russian diesel refineries. (Rebuking Trump, Zelensky told the Financial Times today that Ukraine will keep attacking refineries anyway.) Although it’s true that the war in Eastern Europe has contributed to higher diesel prices, experts agree that the bigger culprit is the war in Iran

As a stopgap measure, Trump temporarily lifted some restrictions on tax-exempt diesel use, and he made a controversial deal with Russia over the weekend to import potentially millions of tons of diesel
The agreement has been widely denounced as a betrayal of a U.S. ally during wartime, and analysts are doubtful that it will be enough to get prices down
Trump has lately been urging voters to look away from the economic reality, even promising to hand out millions of $5,000 checks if Republicans hold on to their majority in the midterm elections
Judging by the forecasts for his party’s races, Americans aren’t listening
Related: Everything Trump wants to do causes inflation

Now he’s calling the idea a “con job.” Here are three new stories from The Atlantic : 0 for 26: The Trump administration’s astonishing losing record A lab-leak story you haven’t heard Ukraine finds a new set of targets

Today’s News President Trump canceled Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream the December 3 execution of Nidal Malik Hasan, the former Army officer convicted of killing 13 people in the 2009 Fort Hood shooting
The execution will proceed by firing squad, and only immediate family members of the victims will be allowed to witness it in person

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said in an interview with the Financial Times that America had threatened to withhold intelligence and had restricted military-satellite communications, though Trump denied having cut off intelligence-sharing and Ukraine said that Starlink service had been restored

title: The Memory Shortage Comes for Schools
excerpt: For today’s high schoolers, a typical school day from a decade ago must seem like something from the Dark Ages
body: For today’s high schoolers, a typical school day from a decade ago must seem like something from the Dark Ages

These days, students are issued digital textbooks instead of physical ones, they learn how to conduct chemistry experiments through apps that simulate a science lab, and they take standardized tests on a Chromebook
All of this is the result of many years of frenzied investment in ed tech, capped by a pandemic that forced virtual learning
The overwhelming majority of schools nationwide provide each student with their own laptop or tablet
All of these screens have changed the dynamic of the classroom
When a student is supposed to be using their school-issued iPad to diligently take notes during math class, they might instead be messaging a friend
Across the country, some parents and teachers are mounting a backlash against screens in the classroom
In April, the Los Angeles school board voted to stop giving devices to its youngest students and implemented screen-time limits for all grades
But other schools are pulling back on ed tech for an entirely different reason
Chromebooks, like essentially all other consumer electronics, need RAM, or random-access memory
So do the data centers that power every conversation with a chatbot
The AI industry is using so many memory chips that it’s led to a global shortage, making gadgets much more expensive
For an individual consumer, the memory crunch— RAMaggedon , if you will—means having to spend a few hundred dollars more on a new computer
But school districts, many of which are already cash-strapped, buy hundreds or thousands of computers every year
The administrators I spoke with for this story told me that they have had to scramble to acquire all the electronics they now need

As RAMaggedon drags on, they said, something has got to give. [ Read: If you need a laptop, buy it now ] Schools started picking up on the memory shortage last winter, months before most of the country
They have to figure out bulk orders for laptops and tablets long before the academic year begins

Many of them turn to third-party vendors, which have typically provided quotes that are locked in for a month, giving technology directors time to secure the funds from their districts to make purchases that can run millions of dollars

As memory prices have soared, Mark Samberg, the chief technology officer of Chatham County Schools in North Carolina, is hearing a different message from his vendors. “Now quotes are going to be good for 48 hours, a week, or 14 days,” he told me
Samberg scooped up the Chromebooks he could find
In March, a Chromebook vendor warned Homewood-Flossmoor High School in Illinois that its prices would be going up soon

Steve Richardson, the district’s IT director, quickly placed an order, only to be eventually told it couldn’t be fulfilled because memory chips were on back order. “We were kind of in dire straits,” Richardson told me
In 2023, Chromebooks cost the school $353 a piece
The price rose to $400, then $412, and then $427
The most recent batch that Richardson purchased, in August, cost $508 each
But the district needed them to ensure that every student had a Chromebook ahead of the PSAT, which is now entirely digital
So far, schools have been willing to stomach the costs to continue giving every student a device
Districts initially decided to implement “one to one” policies on the premise that technology can be an equalizing force in the classroom; many educators and administrators still believe that
Dorann Avey, the board chair of the State Educational Technology Directors Association, told me that she is concerned that RAMaggedon will widen the digital divide

Devices are not for “just writing papers,” she said. “We’re trying to prepare students to learn different software that is workplace- and workforce-appropriate.” That has meant making difficult trade-offs
Because of the extra spending on laptops for students, Homewood-Flossmoor didn’t buy any new smart whiteboards or computers for teachers this year
In Texas, the Paradise Independent School District has considered asking students to bring in their own laptop or tablet, Director of Technology Doug Bryant told me
A common solution has been to extend the lifetime of a laptop
Instead of replacing a device every four years, schools are opting for seven or eight to reduce how many units they need to purchase in a given year
But that introduces new problems: Older computers sometimes aren’t able to update to the latest operating system, which could create cybersecurity risks
Schools are already a top target for hackers, because they store lots of sensitive personal information but have limited resources
Plus, as a device gets older, its battery degrades and may ultimately need to be replaced
That costs “time and money,” Avey said. “But it’s still less money than buying brand-new devices.” All of this may not be enough
Multiple administrators told me that they are already considering rolling back their one-to-one device policies because of RAMaggedon, and the challenges for schools are poised to mount
Heading into this school year, some districts were able to skirt the worst of the memory shortage by buying Chromebooks before prices really started to soar

title: A Bold Era in Hollywood Ends With a Whimper
excerpt: Sign up for Video Village , a new weekly newsletter in which David Sims unearths cinematic gems and brings readers into his movie obsession
body: Sign up for Video Village , a new weekly newsletter in which David Sims unearths cinematic gems and brings readers into his movie obsession
To kick off this newsletter, I sent out a message declaring that movies were “ undeniably back .” Within days, it seemed that the sky was falling again
Two venerable studios, Paramount and Warner Bros
Discovery, officially merged on October 6, further consolidating power in Hollywood into just a few conglomerates
The new entity has been dubbed Skydance, the name of the original production company that CEO David Ellison founded in 2006
Not much has outwardly changed thus far, new moniker aside
But internally, Ellison has already made at least one concerning decision
Once the deal closed, two key leaders at Warner Bros., the bolder and more risk-taking of the two studios, were immediately shown the door: Michael De Luca and Pam Abdy, the co-chairs of Warner Bros
Their departure suggested what many industry analysts had feared: that their new boss was no longer a fan of taking big, bold risks
After all, the news that De Luca and Abdy were exiting the company —to be replaced by Paramount’s current team, which will oversee what has been referred to as the “Paramount Warner Bros
Motion Picture unit” (try saying that three times fast)—arrived right before a historically bad weekend for the studio

The Tom Cruise project Digger opened on October 2 to only $8 million domestically, on a budget that reportedly climbed as high as $180 million; that’s an especially anemic number given Cruise’s involvement as both star and co-producer
Digger now stands as Warner Bros.’ final release before it joined Skydance, and the movie’s catastrophic box-office performance is the latest in a series of tough beats for the company this year
Given the film’s wild ambition, its failure will also be a fitting coda for an era that was very up-and-down financially—but often creatively thrilling
Pictures in 2022, bringing with them a strategic reset

They were both well-regarded names in the world of awards-friendly indie cinema, shaking up a studio that was bouncing back from a theatrical strategy unpopular with the industry: putting blockbusters on HBO Max the day they were released

De Luca was a storied executive whose career included green-lighting boundary-pushing projects by Paul Thomas Anderson and David Fincher and earning Best Picture Oscar nominations for such movies as The Social Network and Moneyball
Abdy started out her career at Danny Devito’s hyper-cool Jersey Films and worked on The Revenant and The Big Short , among other awards-season hits, as president of the production outfit New Regency

Together, they presided over a splashy period at Warner Bros. in which they focused on recruiting big stars and major auteurs while they also shed the remains of the prior leadership’s flailing, expensive approach to the DC Comics franchise
But their results were inconsistent: In 2023, the giant success of Barbie in the summer and Wonka at Christmastime buoyed the studio
The following year, Furiosa: A Mad Max Saga and Joker: Folie à Deux were such expensive flops that industry experts began predicting De Luca and Abdy would soon lose their jobs
Instead, last year, the duo spearheaded a cinematic slate that will likely be spoken about in hushed tones in Hollywood C-suites for generations
A Minecraft Movie took advantage of its kid-friendly IP to make nearly $1 billion worldwide, despite being barely coherent
The relaunch of the DC cinematic universe went splendidly with Superman , directed by the new DC Studios co-chair, James Gunn
The silly sequels Final Destination Bloodlines and The Conjuring: Last Rites punched above their weight commercially
Zach Cregger’s Weapons was not just a horror hit but also a critical favorite that won major awards
Ryan Coogler’s Sinners , whose high budget met prerelease skepticism from box-office analysts, was a cultural sensation and a financial boon
And Anderson’s blockbuster, One Battle After Another , earned just enough money to justify its scale before taking the Oscar for Best Picture
In basically each of these cases, De Luca and Abdy’s calculation of betting on creators who had an established track record and pairing them with reliable stars worked
Meanwhile, safe comic-book and video-game adaptations helped shore up any business concerns
This year, however, the same approach has resulted in a lot of swings and misses

Collaborations between acclaimed directors and performers, such as Maggie Gyllenhaal and Jessie Buckley’s The Bride! , failed to make back their budget; Supergirl and Practical Magic 2 were box-office disappointments, in part because of poor reviews
Warner Bros. couldn’t even claim the surprise success of Coyote vs
Acme , a Looney Tunes movie that it sold to the indie distributor Ketchup Entertainment after deciding in 2023 not to release it ; it became a sleeper family hit this summer
Maybe Digger flopping was the final straw for Ellison
Or maybe the Skydance CEO was always intent on keeping his own team in charge
Paramount has adopted a more populist, risk-averse strategy since Ellison took over that studio in 2025

This year’s schedule included crowd-pleasing horror films and a Jackass clip-show-style sequel, although none was particularly successful with theatergoers; a new live-action Street Fighter and the latest edition in the Angry Birds franchise are on the way

Indeed, it even has a Tom Cruise movie on the slate for 2028—but rather than being an auteurist effort like Digger , it’s a sequel to the 1990 NASCAR drama Days of Thunder that I’d argue nobody was really asking for
Skydance seems to be planning to keep Paramount and Warner Bros. separate, the industry reporter Matthew Belloni suggested in a Puck column last week

title: This Is Edgar Allan Poe, and I Am Begging Kelly Clarkson to Take My Bird
excerpt: I have read that you wanted a bird but were not permitted to obtain it
body: I have read that you wanted a bird but were not permitted to obtain it
Well, I am in possession of a bird and do not want to be
Perhaps we could come to a mutually beneficial arrangement
It sits, croaking, uninvited, on my bust of Pallas. (I would also be happy to give you the bust of Pallas
It is a tasteful bust; my only qualm with it is that it reminds me of my lost Lenore.) I didn’t ask the bird to be here
To the contrary, I would like nothing more than for it to depart
I have asked it to do so, first politely, and then rudely
When I read of your encounter with the store Art of Play I felt the only hint of hope I had felt for quite some time
I will tell her the situation, and we can wring some triumph out of this whole miserable thing
How did I come by this bird? Oh, the usual way
You’re pondering, weak and weary, many and many a quaint and curious volume of forgotten lore
Then you hear a tapping, as of someone gently rapping, rapping at your chamber door? Well, this happened to me recently
And now the accursed thing will not depart! I want to be rid of the bird
I understand that the bird in which you expressed interest is a windup bird
Is that anything? I understand that the bird in which you were interested is named Molly

You could call it anything if only you would take the demonic thing out of here! Before you object that the kind of bird you want is inanimate, whereas mine is clearly a live bird, I have considered this, and I think that the main objection people have to a live bird indoors is that the bird will fly around disruptively and try to escape
I have said, “Shoo, bird.” I have said sterner things, things that I now regret
It just sits there and says, “Nevermore,” at intervals
Also, its sable hue would go with anything
Looking at this bird from an interior-design perspective, I think it would fit any room, especially if I included the bust, which, again, I am willing to do
Do you need to feed it? I have not gotten that far with the bird
I think maybe it sustains itself by other means
It just sits there saying, “Nevermore.” Make no mistake, I am not offering you a free bird because I doubt your ability to pay
I am offering you a bird because I hate the infernal creature and want it out of my sight! But I would accept your money
Using that money, I could perhaps even get rid of the beating heart that seems to be stuck in my wall

title: What the Falling Leaves Taught Thoreau
excerpt: This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic ’s archives to contextualize the present
body: This is an edition of Time-Travel Thursdays, a journey through The Atlantic ’s archives to contextualize the present
Published in the October 1862 issue of The Atlantic , Henry David Thoreau’s essay “Autumnal Tints” arrived in a season of death

The Civil War was well into its second year, and copies of the magazine began reaching readers shortly after the Battle of Antietam, on September 17, a day with the grim distinction of being the single bloodiest of the conflict
Thoreau himself was already gone, having died four months earlier, a casualty not of war but of tuberculosis
Thoreau’s essay makes no connection between the fall and the conditions of fighting, as the poet John Greenleaf Whittier did in “ The Battle Autumn of 1862 ,” in the same issue

Instead, Thoreau’s work is a written version of what he’d initially imagined as a visual book—one in which he would compile the leaves of all the trees around him and follow their progression through the colors, from green to brown. (The magazine included a simple engraving of a scarlet-oak leaf that he had rendered.) He had first drafted “Autumnal Tints” as a lecture in the 1850s, before the war’s start, and delivered a version of it in what would be the final public talk of his life

The event was far from a resounding success—a local newspaper deemed it “dull, commonplace and unsatisfactory”—and making the trip to Waterbury, Connecticut, in the bitter cold of December 1860 had worsened an illness from which Thoreau would never recover

The revised copy that appeared in The Atlantic gave the story new and enduring life. “If I were to live, I should have much to report on Natural History generally,” Thoreau wrote in a March 1862 letter, a few months before his death
As it was, weak and barely able to breathe, he could do little more than adapt some of his lectures into essays for The Atlantic with the help of his sister Sophia
The enterprise marked a reconciliation with the magazine

In 1858, the first installment of his “Chesuncook” essay had appeared in the June issue, minus one beloved sentence about a fallen pine tree: “It is as immortal as I am, and perchance will go to as high a heaven, there to tower above me still.” He was incensed when he found the line unceremoniously axed from the printed copy. “Is this the avowed character of the Atlantic Monthly?” he demanded in a letter to the editor, James Russell Lowell. “I should like an early reply.” No reply, early or late, was forthcoming
Making matters worse, neither was Thoreau’s payment, which he’d already deemed lower than what he deserved
It took two additional letters to secure the $198 he was due
Fields as The Atlantic ’s editor in 1861 cleared the way for new contributions from Thoreau
Fields had first printed Walden seven years earlier at his publishing house, and he suggested another collaboration

Thoreau agreed, on much more favorable financial terms than most of the magazine’s other contributors, and on the condition that “no sentiment or sentence be altered or omitted without my consent.” As Thoreau prepared the manuscripts for Fields, he confessed to a friend an inclination to expunge some of the humor from his writing, noting that “I cannot bear the levity I find.” But much levity does remain in “Autumnal Tints.” It is, on the whole, a joyous celebration of the season, and an invitation to “wild delight.” Through his observations, he divined that “man’s spirits should rise as high as Nature’s,—should hang out their flag, and the routine of his life be interrupted by an analogous expression of joy and hilarity.” As he worked through a catalog of trees and plants, he contrasted his own careful appreciation of the natural world around him (“The expression of this grass haunted me for a week”) with the bustle of his neighbors amid the busy occupations of the harvest

Stopping to take in the brilliant hues of the elms lining the Concord Common, he wondered “if there is any answering ripeness in the lives of the men who live beneath them.” Death, however, is never far from “Autumnal Tints.” Keenly aware of his own imminent demise as he revised this manuscript for publication, Thoreau saw his mortality everywhere in the season

Walking on dead leaves in the forest, he imagined the setting as a grand and consecrated cemetery. “They that soared so loftily,” Thoreau wrote of the leaves, “how contentedly they return to dust again, and are laid low, resigned to lie and decay at the foot of the tree, and afford nourishment to new generations of their kind, as well as to flutter on high! They teach us how to die.” Thoreau, still seeking joy on the verge of his own death, had learned the lesson well.

title: Winners of the Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026
excerpt: © James Lewin / Wildlife Photographer of the Year The Meeting Place
body: © James Lewin / Wildlife Photographer of the Year The Meeting Place
James Lewin watched a young bull elephant spray a group of zebra as they congregated in the Kenyan Chyulu Hills
Although there was no shortage of subjects and action around this waterhole, James had to deal with the harsh, unforgiving light
He chose to soften the light using a camera converted to infrared, creating this dreamlike scene. © Anton Sorokin / Wildlife Photographer of the Year Protective Pose
Winner, Behavior: Amphibians and Reptiles
Anton Sorokin found a California newt laying its eggs as it clasped vegetation that already held another newt’s egg clutch. © Alex Visbal / Wildlife Photographer of the Year The Great Divide
Alex Visbal documented how a single engineered line can reshape an entire wetland in Utah’s Great Salt Lake
The distinctive pink color on the left is caused by bright-pink microbes that thrive in extremely saline water, which happens when an area is cut off from a supply of fresh water
The lake’s ecology is in sharp decline because of industrial use, upstream diversions, and climate change
Since this image was taken, the State of Utah has brought the area under conservation management. © Loren Elliott / Wildlife Photographer of the Year On the Outskirts
A coyote pads along a trail in Bernal Heights Park, overlooking the city and bay of San Francisco

This individual is part of a resident pack that Loren Elliott observed hunting rodents in the park, which is also popular with people and dogs. © Tony Wu / Wildlife Photographer of the Year Making Morays
Tony Wu provides a first-time glimpse into the mating ritual of Abbott’s moray eels
Wu has been working with biologists to address a knowledge gap of the social behavior of this eel species

Guided only by a dim red-light source to minimize disturbance, and using a customized fisheye camera lens, he has studied this male since 2024 as it visits females that dwell in crevices on the reef. © Kutub Uddin / Wildlife Photographer of the Year Tiny Dancers
Kutub Uddin reveals a magical and often surreal world of slime molds that can barely be seen with the naked eye

Fine threads, known as capillitium , emerge on the round, yellow-green bodies, which will eventually help disperse reproductive spores. © Francisco Negroni / Wildlife Photographer of the Year Warning Sign
Francisco Negroni recorded this scene of a dead puma amid the rugged, windswept beauty of Argentine Patagonia

Tied to the fence and presented as a hunting trophy, this display was one that Francisco had “never witnessed or photographed before.” In 2025, Santa Cruz banned the hunting of pumas, but illegal persecution continues. © Aaron Sanders / Wildlife Photographer of the Year A Watchful Eye
Aaron Sanders glimpsed a common octopus behind a curtain of kelp in the waters off southwest England

Sanders was diving off Porthkerris Beach when he noticed the footprints of octopus suckers through a thin blade of kelp, and a single eye slowly emerging. “We remained perfectly still, watching one another with a seemingly shared curiosity,” Sanders said. © Oscar Whitfield / Wildlife Photographer of the Year Labour of Love
Winner, 11-14 Years, Young Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026
Oscar Whitfield noticed the arduous exertion of this dung beetle pushing its precious cargo

Using a fast shutter speed and high light sensitivity, Oscar lay flat on the ground to photograph the beetle at eye level, with the sunshine and heat creating dry dust all around him. © Alex Lindbloom / Wildlife Photographer of the Year Night-Time Catch
Alex Lindbloom found a whale shark investigating the catch of a “bagan,” or mobile net-fishing platform, in the inky waters off Papua
Alex started searching for sharks around dawn when the nets were still in the water
Initially lacking natural light for his drone’s camera, he found these sharks illuminated by the bagan’s bright lights. © Isak Pretorius / Wildlife Photographer of the Year Scenes from the Swamp
Isak Pretorius chanced across two elusive shoebill storks among wetland vegetation
Exploring the swamp in a narrow canoe with a guide, Isak felt exceptionally lucky to see not one but two shoebills
The birds pulled out vegetation, dropped it, and then repeated the process several times
It’s likely that this was a breeding pair gathering nesting material. © Federico Veronesi / Wildlife Photographer of the Year The Aftermath
Winner, Behavior: Mammals, and Overall Winner, Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026
Federico Veronesi witnessed this powerful moment of an elephant carrying a dead calf, a rare glimpse into complex animal behaviors
Veronesi was tracking elephants when he came across an unusual pattern of drag marks in the sand of a dry riverbed
The source became clear when he caught up with a family group
A female emerged with the calf, its leg wedged between her tusk and trunk
Behaviors centering on death have been observed in both Asian and African elephants, including vocalizations, guarding the dead, inspecting and handling bones, and carrying the deceased

Some researchers suggest these behaviors could indicate an elephant’s journey to understanding death, while others interpret these actions as possible displays of grief. © Michał Michalski / Wildlife Photographer of the Year Escape Artistry
Michał Michalski used a slow shutter speed to create the illusion of trees still swathed in autumn foliage
Michalski was in a field of unharvested sunflowers that had attracted mixed flocks of birds, especially goldfinches and bramblings

title: How much more can nuclear power plants give?
excerpt: Squeezing more out of existing reactors: Nuclear operators are investing billions to boost output from plants already on the grid, a process called a power upra
body: Squeezing more out of existing reactors: Nuclear operators are investing billions to boost output from plants already on the grid, a process called a power uprate
Constellation alone plans to spend $4.3 billion across 11 reactors, adding enough capacity to power roughly 700,000 homes
Big Tech is footing the bill: Long-term electricity deals with Google and Meta are helping to make these expensive upgrades financially viable

The math still falls short: Even if every possible uprate in the US were completed, the added capacity would cover only a fraction of the 30 gigawatts of new peak demand that AI is expected to create by 2030 within PJM's grid alone. " data-chronoton-post-id="1146577" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> In this age of rising electricity demand, people are trying to squeeze every last bit of power out of every power plant possible
Over the past few weeks, there’s been big news about nuclear power plants trying to do just that
Constellation, the largest nuclear operator in the US, announced plans to add nearly a gigawatt of new capacity across 11 existing nuclear reactors at six plants
And on October 5, the Department of Energy awarded a $4.2 billion loan to Vistra for previously announced upgrades at three plants
Pushing existing reactors to produce more could help provide more clean power for data centers, quickly
But just how much additional power can we count on? Upgrading equipment at existing nuclear power plants can allow them to reach a higher capacity; the process is called a power uprate

Operators have been doing this since the 1970s in the US, but it’s been less common in recent years as demand for electricity plateaued and cheap natural gas put financial pressure on nuclear power plants
Some plants closed, and putting in more money to produce more electricity didn’t make much sense at others
Between 2001 and 2010, the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission approved over 80 uprates
But with the rise of AI and the related boom in electricity demand, there’s been a shift
We’re seeing shuttered plants like Palisades and Three Mile Island race to reopen
And existing plants are looking to uprate again
Some uprates are minor, involving changes to instrument setpoints or calculations at the plant
But more major overhauls, which can boost reactor power by as much as 20%, require replacing plant equipment
Generally, uprates involve using fuel that’s more highly enriched, or a higher volume of fresh fuel, in the nuclear reactor
That helps produce more steam, which is used to turn a turbine and generate electricity
To handle that additional energy, the main turbines and equipment such as pumps, motors, generators, and transformers are upgraded
The most recent major uprate approved in the US was for three reactors at the Browns Ferry nuclear power plant in Alabama
A $475 million project saw that plant expand its power capacity by 14% between 2018 and 2019
Constellation announced plans this week to spend more than $4.3 billion on uprates to 11 reactors
The additional electricity will be enough to power roughly 700,000 US homes
Google agreed to buy electricity from these plants, and the 20-year agreement was a major factor in making the uprates happen

As Joe Dominguez, Constellation’s CEO, told the New York Times : “These are capital intensive, labor intensive projects that require a different price point than the market trades at, frankly.” Also in the last few weeks, the US Department of Energy shared that it will commit over $4 billion to help finance upgrades and modernization for Vistra nuclear power plants across Pennsylvania and Ohio
Those projects will add 433 megawatts of power capacity, and Meta has already signed on to buy electricity from the plants in a long-term deal

A note about cost: On a per-kilowatt basis, that Constellation project is less expensive than building a new reactor, but it’s still more expensive than building a new utility-scale solar farm with energy storage or a combined-cycle natural-gas plant
Even at this high cost, uprates are in high demand
Today, the US nuclear fleet has roughly 98 gigawatts of total power capacity
Depending on who you ask, there’s somewhere between three and eight additional gigawatts on the table from uprates
A pretty significant chunk of the potential uprates in the US are already accounted for—the NRC already expects applications to add 2.4 gigawatts of power to reactors through 2032
It’s crucial to put these plans (and the total potential for uprates in the US) in perspective, though
PJM, the grid operator that covers much of the East Coast, expects about 30 gigawatts of additional peak demand because of AI by 2030
All the possible nationwide nuclear uprates would cover just a fraction of that
Making the most of existing nuclear reactors is a relatively easy win at a time when we need all the zero-emissions power we can get
But there’s still a lot of demand, and if we want more nuclear power to meet it, eventually that will require actually building new reactors
This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter
To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here .

title: Six wild ideas for perpetuating your mind
excerpt: Have you ever thought about what makes you you ? Science assures us it has everything to do with the three-pound organ between our ears, with its billions of ne
body: Have you ever thought about what makes you you ? Science assures us it has everything to do with the three-pound organ between our ears, with its billions of neurons and trillions of delicate connections
But it’s a lot trickier to explain why we have a sense of self-awareness or to pin down precisely where that first memory of Mommy actually resides
As we age, we forget most of what we’ve experienced, yet there’s still undeniable continuity: At 30, or 50, or 70, you will still be you
To preserve that elusive continuity of self, some far-thinking technologists are working on ways to keep your brain going—even beyond death
Let’s call them the “mind savers.” They’re exploring everything from freezing brains in liquid nitrogen to augmenting living ones to uploading our memories to the cloud
Here, we look at six possible paths for keeping your mind going, how feasible they’d be, and what benefits the ­present-day research might bring—even if cognitive immortality doesn’t pan out
EDDIE GUY Head transplant White’s experiments have been a source of grim fascination ever since

But to a few neuroscientists they’re inspiration, suggesting that one day a human head transplant—or, as some call it, a body transplant—could succeed.  The idea’s main proponent is Sergio Canavero, a controversial Italian surgeon who, 10 years ago, even claimed he’d found a volunteer in Valery Spiridinov, a computer programmer suffering from a degenerative muscle disease
Spiridinov initially agreed to have his head transferred to the body of a brain-dead donor in China, but he later bowed out of the plan and instead got married
Critics say the procedure would be more like murder than medicine
Or, best-case scenario: Volunteers would be left paralyzed and in need of a ventilator for life.  Canavero says that’s not necessarily true
He claims people’s views on the operation will change once they accept that reconnecting severed spinal cords is already possible
He pointed MIT Technology Review to a research article from this past summer that he coauthored with surgeons at Moscow’s Sklifosovsky Research and Clinical Institute for Emergency Medicine
The team cut through the spinal cords of three pigs at a point midway along their backs and then tested whether the severed nerve bodies could be fused back together using a surgical sealant
According to that paper, which appeared in the journal PLOS One , all the pigs regained the ability to stand and even walk unsteadily
Does that mean a head could be attached to a new body and then actually control it? Mainstream researchers aren’t convinced

Grégoire Courtine, a spinal rehabilitation specialist at the École Polytechnique Fédérale de Lausanne in Switzerland, says he’s been following Canavero’s claims “with little respect” and thinks that we should “pay zero attention.” “There is no technology … capable of such a crazy idea,” Courtine wrote in an email
Mindclones Just 12 years after the book came out, artificial-intelligence technology has already brought some of her predictions to “life,” so to speak

Services such as StoryFile, Afterlife AI, and Synthesia allow users to upload their personal information and likeness in order to produce either conversational bots that share their memories or video talking heads that sound (and look) exactly like them
Influencers now let their “AI clones” do their work on TikTok, and some people are even building avatars of their aging parents in order to preserve their personalities
While this mimicry can produce comical results, unhealthy attachments, or uncanny vibes, the increasing realism of generative AI invites people to emotionally accept the avatars as real beings

That was the case when Rothblatt appeared as a digital avatar during a 2025 event held by the UCLA Department of Communication called “The Bridge to Humanizing AI.” Her copy, named Marvatar, was projected on a screen, led the discussions, and talked with the meatspace Rothblatt as an equal, at one point saying, “The dance isn’t about who leads, but how we move together.” According to the university, attendees were “visibly moved” and wept “with wonder” at Rothblatt’s vision of digital equality

What’s still missing from Rothblatt’s mindclone prediction is evidence that these avatars have—or ever will have—any kind of true self-awareness. (We asked ChatGPT if it’s conscious, and it answered , “Probably not.”) But all that remains a gray zone

Neuroscientists don’t have a clear definition of consciousness, much less a diagnostic test they could apply to an avatar.  Instead, what if the final determination is in the eye of the beholder? Your digital clone might not be you

But at some point it might be good enough for me.  Brain in a jar So, campy sci-fi film lovers that we are, it got our attention last year when a company called Bexorg started showing journalists actual human brains in vats, which it has been acquiring from organ donors soon after death and then “rebooting” by infusing them with oxygen-rich artificial blood
The company claims these “physiologically intact human brains” will be more useful than animals for drug testing and safer than trying experiments on living volunteers
Add an Alzheimer’s compound to one of these disembodied brains and researchers can then measure exactly what the drug does inside the organ
Bexorg’s CEO, Zvonimir Vrselja, is “sure” that some people would like to restore consciousness to out-of-body brains, but he’s tried to douse such speculation
While they are metabolically active, the company says, the brains have lost all coordinated electrical activity

That means they aren’t conscious—although, just to make sure, the neuroscientists running the experiments add the strong anesthetic propofol to the tissues.  What’s more, right now a brain can be kept “alive” outside the body for only about 24 hours
Still, efforts are underway to improve the life-support systems
Bexorg says it hopes to eventually keep its brains going for two weeks
EDDIE GUY Gradual brain replacement On paper, the goal is to manufacture tissue to graft into the brains of stroke victims, reversing damage and restoring function

Less officially, the project’s existence is a surprise coup for an extreme plan to defeat aging advanced by Jean Hébert, the neuroscientist leading the program, who argued in his 2020 book, Replacing Aging , that we can live longer by replacing our aging brain cells with young ones
That’s why—according to Hébert—it would have to happen gradually, in small chunks, so our brains would have time to adapt to the new tissue
Scientists who applied for the program say Hébert insisted on a very specific technological approach

While most researchers engineer individual cell types, ARPA-H asked for complex chunks of young, functional cortex—more or less like what you’d find in a developing fetus. “He wanted to create essentially an embryonic form of cortex that he thought you could somehow graft into an adult brain,” says Marius Wernig, a Stanford University stem-cell researcher who applied
Skeptics say it’s unknown whether replacement brain chunks will ever properly function as part of your brain—say, by taking over memories
What’s more, it’s still unclear how to manufacture youthful cortex, or what ARPA-H calls “neocortical precursor tissue,” in the lab
One idea is to employ the latest advances in brain organoids

title: Pig kidneys that were “frozen” for a year have been brought back to life
excerpt: Frozen kidneys brought back to life: Scientists have successfully vitrified pig kidneys—cooling them to -150°C—and rewarmed them after up to a year in storage
body: Frozen kidneys brought back to life: Scientists have successfully vitrified pig kidneys—cooling them to -150°C—and rewarmed them after up to a year in storage
The kidneys regained color and produced urine, key signs they were working

Nanoparticles are the secret ingredient: Iron oxide nanoparticles infused into the organs allow for rapid, even rewarming when activated by an electromagnetic field—solving one of cryobiology's longest-standing technical headaches

A revolution for transplantation: Long-term organ banking could mean organs wait for patients, not the other way around—giving doctors time to better match donors and recipients and potentially reduce the need for lifelong immune-suppressing drugs

Still not ready for prime time: The rewarmed kidneys showed signs of injury, likely from toxic cryoprotectant chemicals, and produced less urine than expected. " data-chronoton-post-id="1146091" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Pig kidneys that were cooled to -150 °C and stored in a freezer for months have been successfully rewarmed and shown to work again for the first time, say scientists
They hope to replicate the findings with human organs
The kidneys—which are similar in size to human ones—were left in a glass-like state, in one case for over a year

Once they had been rewarmed, tested in machines, and transplanted into pigs, the kidneys regained their color and made urine—key signs they were working. “Ten years ago … I wouldn’t say I had high hopes it was actually going to work,” says Erik Finger, a transplant surgeon at the University of Minnesota who co-led the work. “After we did the last transplant, I walked out of the room and said, ‘This is a big deal.’” The research was shared at the preprint server bioRxiv and has not yet been peer-reviewed
The kidneys aren’t perfect, and the researchers have yet to demonstrate that they can sustain life over the long term

But the results represent a milestone achievement, say others in the field. “Thank God that someone’s actually managed to do it in one organ and prove that it works,” says Peter Kilbride, a cryobiologist and cofounder of Kyros Kairos, a company focused on improving funding for cryopreservation research, who was not involved in the research. “For years, people have been trying and failing to get to this step

Finally, we’ve got this breakthrough.” “Their work is amazing and will enable us to truly, indefinitely bank organs,” says Korkut Uygun, a biomedical engineer and professor of surgery at Harvard Medical School, who was also not involved in the research. “It is a revolutionary time for transplantation.” Buying time Every year, tens of thousands of organ transplants take place in the US alone
These procedures are thought to have saved 2 million years of life in the last 25 years
But there’s plenty of room for improvement
One major challenge is the lack of available organs
Even when an organ becomes available, it can be difficult to get it to the right recipient within 24 to 36 hours, which is the current limit for preserving human organs
People who receive organ transplants must also take drugs that suppress their immune systems for the rest of their lives
These drugs are meant to stop their bodies from rejecting the new organs
But they come with side effects and increase the risk of infections and cancer
The ability to bank organs for long periods of time holds the promise to address all these challenges
Doctors would have more time to match organs to recipients

They’d be able to limit the risk of organ rejection, too—potentially by preparing recipients, and their immune systems, beforehand. “With real organ banking … instead of the patients waiting for the organ, it’s the organs that are waiting for the patients,” says Finger
Scientists have been able to cool cells to ultra-low temperatures through a process called vitrification, which essentially turns them to something like glass
This procedure is already used to store eggs, sperm, and embryos
Some problems can be avoided with cryoprotectants—chemicals that work like antifreeze and prevent damaging ice crystals from forming
But these chemicals tend to be incredibly toxic
It’s also difficult to rapidly and uniformly cool large tissues, and just as hard to evenly rewarm an organ all the way through
Working with John Bischof, a bioengineer at the University of Minnesota, Finger and colleagues have come up with a solution
Once an organ has been loaded with a cryoprotectant, they infuse it with iron oxide nanoparticles
These nanoparticles don’t do anything to the cells

But when it’s time to rewarm the organ, they can be activated with an electromagnetic field.  When the radiofrequency of that field switches between two states, the particles also flip, realigning themselves with the field
That causes them to release heat throughout the organ

Adjusting the power of the field allows the team to control the rate of heating so that it gets faster once the organ reaches -120°C.  The researchers successfully vitrified rat kidneys using this approach in work published in 2023
Back then, they were able to rewarm kidneys that had been kept in a freezer for up to 100 days before transplanting them into rats
Since then, the team has been trying to achieve the same success with bigger organs
Pig kidneys are thought to be a good model for human ones—they’re about the same size and look similar
Rat kidneys weigh around one gram; pig kidneys are around 100

The cryoprotectant used for vitrifying rat kidneys didn’t work as well in the pig organs. “We had to rediscover and modify the cocktail,” says Bischof. “That’s why it’s taken us three years.” Deep-freezing kidneys The first step in the procedure is to remove a kidney from a donor pig

Once it’s out, the kidney is flushed with a commonly used organ preservation solution to remove the blood, bagged, and temporarily laid on a bed of ice in a cooler so it can be taken over to the engineering lab
There, team members unpack the kidney and hook it up to a device they’ve designed to control the organ’s temperature and pressure
Then they start to load it up with the cocktail of cryoprotectants, slowly enough to ensure an even spread through the organ but quickly enough to minimize any toxic effects

title: Using light to control brain cells – neuroscientist Karl Deisseroth explains how he made his Nobel-winning discovery
url:
<title>Using light to control brain cells – neuroscientist Karl Deisseroth explains how he made his Nobel-winning discovery</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765692/original/file-20261012-50-iclyvu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C166%2C2000%2C1333&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Optogenetics involves the use of light to alter the activity of neurons.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/illustration/glowing-fiber-optics-on-brain-scan-royalty-free-illustration/2287907473">Westend61/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p><em>The <a href="https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2026/press-release/">2026 Nobel Prize in physiology or medicine</a> honored <a href="https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2026/deisseroth/facts/">Karl Deisseroth</a>, <a href="https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2026/hegemann/facts/">Peter Hegemann</a> and <a href="https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2026/nagel/facts/">Georg Nagel</a> for their work developing optogenetics – a technique that allows researchers to control the activity of neurons with light.</em></p>

<p><em>The Conversation Weekly podcast talked to Karl Deisseroth, a neuroscientist at Stanford University, about his journey developing optogenetics and its potential to treat a wide range of neuropsychiatric conditions. What follows is an edited transcript of the podcast.</em></p>

<hr>

<p><strong>Take us back to the early 1990s. You’re training to be a doctor and you start a rotation working with psychiatric patients. What questions about the brain did that raise for you?</strong></p>

<p>Both basic neuroscience (people asking how the brain works) and clinical neuroscience (doctors trying to help people with brain disorders) have faced a very similar problem, which is the brain is quite mysterious and quite hard to study.</p>

<p>It’s billions of fragile, transparent, very fast-acting cells, buried within the skull and doing very complex things. We don’t have a good model for how the brain works, unlike the heart, which is very <a href="https://theconversation.com/engineering-mini-human-hearts-to-study-pregnancy-complications-and-birth-defects-226883">obviously a pump</a>. We don’t actually know what the brain’s trying to do.</p>

<p>A lot of neuropsychiatric treatments are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2021.08.018">not as effective as they could be</a>, and developing new ideas has been hard. The treatments we had were <a href="https://theconversation.com/im-part-of-the-team-writing-the-next-bible-of-psychiatry-for-the-first-time-the-dsm-will-use-biology-to-understand-mental-disorders-288064">not grounded in a solid understanding</a> of the cells involved. What are the cells actually doing? What are they trying to do? This was a problem that held back treatment.</p>

<p>When I was in psychiatry training in the early 2000s, and also as a medical student in the late 1990s, I was very much impressed with the magnitude of the challenge.</p>

<p><strong>You went on to get a Ph.D. in neuroscience, and then you set up a lab at Stanford trying to understand how to control particular cells in the brain. What were the first experiments you did?</strong></p>

<p>I have a background in molecular biology, and I knew how to work with genes. So I was motivated to see if we could use genetics to make a treatment or an intervention that targets one kind of cell.</p>

<p>Every cell has genes that tell it what to do. Different cells in the brain, just as other parts of the body, can be genetically targeted because different cells have different jobs. A cell that is a <a href="https://theconversation.com/dopamine-is-a-brain-chemical-famously-linked-to-mood-and-pleasure-but-researchers-have-found-multiple-types-of-dopamine-neurons-with-different-functions-211985">dopamine neuron</a> has all the machinery needed to make the hormone dopamine. It uses different genes than a cell that makes the hormone serotonin, so they can be distinguished from each other.</p>

<p>And so the thought was maybe I could have a way of controlling just the dopamine cells or just the serotonin cells by inserting a specific gene into them. But I didn’t know what would work well, so I tried inserting different types of genes into neurons.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765686/original/file-20261012-50-qxpafu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Close-up of hand holding an Erlenmeyer flask containing a sample of neon green liquid" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765686/original/file-20261012-50-qxpafu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765686/original/file-20261012-50-qxpafu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765686/original/file-20261012-50-qxpafu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765686/original/file-20261012-50-qxpafu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765686/original/file-20261012-50-qxpafu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765686/original/file-20261012-50-qxpafu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765686/original/file-20261012-50-qxpafu.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Inside this flask is the unicellular algae that played a critical role in the development of optogenetics.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/german-scientist-darius-rauch-holds-a-flask-containing-news-photo/2298094993">Tobias SchwarzSCHWARZ/AFP via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Some of the genes I tried were quite conventional; they were genes from mammals that I thought might affect the activity of neurons. But one was a <a href="https://theconversation.com/how-pond-algae-led-to-a-nobel-prize-and-a-new-way-to-study-the-brain-293579">gene from a single-celled algae</a> – a microbe that converts light to energy. This gene coded for a light-activated protein called channelrhodopsin-2 that Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel identified a few years earlier.</p>

<p>And I thought it was worth a try. It was the least likely to work, but why not try it? </p>

<p>And amazingly, that was the one that worked. The genes that were lower risk didn’t work, and this gene from a single-cell microbe actually did.</p>

<p><strong>Walk us through what you did. You inserted the gene into rat cells, right?</strong></p>

<p>I had a preparation of cultured rodent neurons in a dish – basically a 24-well plate that let me look at many different conditions at the same time in different wells of this plate. This let me test side by side the conventional mammalian genes and this gene from the algae. </p>

<p>So the first step was to get the genes into the cells. Then I exposed some plates of cells to light, while others I did not. I used a test to see which cells had activated.</p>

<p>When I looked across the cells in the screen, I found that the ones that had the algae gene and had gotten light were showing this marker of activation, whereas the others had a much lower signal. That was a really thrilling moment because it showed that this gene from a photosynthetic single-celled organism – almost as far as you can possibly be from mammals evolutionarily – was working beautifully in fragile mammalian neurons.</p>

<p>It was a moment of a lot of pressure and complexity, but also delight. </p>

<hr>

<p><strong>You went on to name your method optogenetics – the ability to control specific nerves using light in the brain – and you soon went on to using it to control living mice in various ways. What was it like in those first few years of working with live animals?</strong></p>

<p>The <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cell.2021.08.018">first experiment</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/nn1525">was in 2004</a>, but we didn’t show that it could <a href="https://doi.org/10.1523/JNEUROSCI.3578-07.2007">control the behavior of freely moving mammals</a> until 2007. So it took almost three years. But that first moment in 2007 was quite uplifting because that showed we had gone a big, big chunk of the way toward making it work.</p>

<p>This was an experiment that was very visible and easy to understand. The right side of the brain controls the left side of the body and attention to the left side of the world. We put in a fiber optic into the right part of a mouse motor cortex – the part that controls movement – and when we flipped the switch, the mouse immediately began going left in circles.</p>

<p>And then as soon as we turned off the laser light, it stopped and just looked up at us, as if nothing had happened. </p>

<p>That, coupled with the first experiment – those were transcendent moments. </p>

<p><strong>What changed in your understanding of the brain in the moment you were able to switch particular neurons on and off?</strong></p>

<p>We understood that the technique would probably work to help us understand the brain better at that moment. And then we immediately started applying it to all sorts of different cells where things were mysterious – where nobody knew or couldn’t prove exactly what one cell type or another was doing in perception and cognition and action.</p>

<p>We were able to find cells that were involved in <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-018-0866-8">hunger</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aan6747">and</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aav3932">thirst</a> – basic survival drives. We were able to identify cells and pathways controlling <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/nature09736">aggression and defensiveness</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/nature13307">parenting</a>, how all the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/nature12018">different parts of anxiety</a> come on together and go away together, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/nature13294">memory</a>, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41593-022-01229-9">motivation</a>. </p>

<p>The general applicability became clear over the subsequent years.</p>

<p><strong>Researchers are now using optogenetics in attempts to restore sight in people with visual impairment. How does that work?</strong></p>

<p>In 2010, two of my colleagues in Europe were interested in delivering one of these light-activated proteins to human eye samples – specifically the <a href="https://www.aao.org/eye-health/anatomy/retina-103">retina of the eye</a> – which worked very well.</p>

<p>So they did careful studies in monkeys and in people. And in 2021, just five years ago, they published a paper showing they could <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-021-01351-4">confer light sensitivity back</a> to the retinas of a person who was completely blind from a neurodegenerative disease called <a href="https://www.nei.nih.gov/eye-health-information/eye-conditions-and-diseases/retinitis-pigmentosa">retinitis pigmentosa</a>.</p>

<p>That’s what we call <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41593-025-02097-9">direct optogenetics</a>. It’s somewhat complicated because you have to deliver the gene and light to the person. </p>

<p><strong>And going back to your psychiatric patients, who you still see in the clinic today, how do you hope optogenetics will be able to help them?</strong></p>

<p>There’s a much easier and more broadly impactful avenue that we call <a href="https://doi.org/10.1038/s41593-025-02097-9">indirect optogenetics</a>, which uses the knowledge that comes from studying which cells matter in a symptom and then designing medications that target those cells. This is something we’ve really lacked in neuropsychiatry for a long time.</p>

<p>Indirect optogenetics is making strong headway for <a href="https://www.fiercebiotech.com/biotech/how-nobel-winning-optogenetics-went-pond-potential-treatments-vision-loss-and-schizophrenia">autism and schizophrenia</a>. There are trials that are moving to their final stages for those disorders.</p>

<p>My particular clinical specialty is autism, and I see the difficulties that come with irritability and anxiety in these patients. And I can see optogenetics leading to new medications that will help.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293926/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>As AI takes on more tasks, what happens when people have to jump in to clean up after it?</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765696/original/file-20261012-50-ssn130.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C8256%2C5504&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">If AI systems have been humming along nicely for weeks or months at a stretch, will the human overseeing them be able to take over when things go wrong?</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/an-alsachilie-employe-monitors-screens-in-the-control-room-news-photo/2243296285">Sebastien Bozon/AFP via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Imagine an artificial intelligence system that has performed reliably for months. Its recommendations are almost always right, and the employee reviewing them has learned that close scrutiny rarely changes the outcome. Then something unusual happens. The AI makes an error or can’t proceed and needs human intervention. The employee is expected to step in and remains responsible for the outcome.</p>

<p>But does the employee know how to do the task? </p>

<p>I’m a <a href="https://www.researchgate.net/scientific-contributions/Murugan-Anandarajan-2180077211">professor of management information systems</a> and the <a href="https://www.lebow.drexel.edu/people/murugananandarajan">academic director</a> of Drexel University’s Center for Applied AI &amp; Business Analytics. In my research on human-AI relationships, I call this latent risk: the possibility that people may lose capabilities their organizations still depend on them to exercise.</p>

<p>AI can continue to perform well while the people overseeing it become less practiced at exercising independent judgment and less prepared to intervene. The risk becomes latent when the organization still depends on that human capability to step in but has little cause to notice that that capability may be weakening.</p>

<p>The concern is not entirely new. The idea of latent risk builds on decades of research into how people respond to automation. For example, <a href="https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2023.1118723">studies of automation bias</a> have shown that people can miss problems or follow automated recommendations even when other evidence suggests they should not. </p>

<p>What is different today is the role AI is beginning to play in organizations. It is beginning to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/23311975.2026.2692205">assume larger parts</a> of the analysis and decision-making that people previously performed.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/9iS-YYLIXiw?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Human in the loop explained.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>The success paradox</h2>

<p>The better AI becomes, the more the nature of human work changes. Work that once required an employee to analyze a problem and reach a decision may instead be performed by AI, leaving the employee to review its recommendation. The employee is no longer doing the same work with AI assistance – rather, their job has shifted from doing the work to overseeing what the AI does.</p>

<p>This shift is already beginning to change how some companies train employees. Accounting giant Deloitte, for example, is <a href="https://www.icaew.com/insights/viewpoints-on-the-news/2026/mar-2026/how-deloitte-is-reshaping-its-audit-training-for-the-ai-age">redesigning its graduate audit training</a> as AI takes over some of the manual work traditionally done by junior auditors. The firm is introducing simulations so trainees can still develop the judgment they will need as they move into more complex work.</p>

<p>More than four decades ago, cognitive psychologist Lisanne Bainbridge described one of the “<a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/00140139.2023.2296176">ironies of automation</a>”: As systems take over more of the work, instead of simply having their work loads lightened, people can be left facing new challenges in monitoring the systems and handling the unusual situations the systems cannot. Later studies found another problem: As people become less involved in a task, they can become less prepared to step in when needed. Researchers have called this the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1518/001872095779064555">out-of-the-loop</a> performance problem.</p>

<p>This reduced involvement may affect more than a person’s readiness to intervene. It can change the capabilities available to the organization.</p>

<p>What work remains for people does not necessarily become easier. It may become harder. These are the situations where experience and independent judgment matter most. The result is a paradox: People may be called upon to exercise independent judgment less often, even as the judgments left to them become more difficult.</p>

<h2>The accountability problem</h2>

<p>Accountability <a href="https://kpmg.com/us/en/media/blogs/2026/q1-ai-pulse-2.html">may not change as quickly</a> as the work does when organizations deploy AI systems. An employee may now oversee far more decisions than they make themselves, while remaining responsible for the outcomes. The organization’s expectations may still reflect how the work was divided before AI took on a larger role. The organization can therefore end up holding people accountable for decisions over which they have less control. </p>

<p>This creates a mismatch. Research on <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s43681-022-00167-3">meaningful human control</a> suggests that responsibility should match a person’s authority and ability to act. An employee may retain the authority to override an AI recommendation and remain responsible for the outcome, yet lose the capability to do so. Authority, responsibility and capability can begin to separate.</p>

<p>Latent risk becomes an organizational design problem, not simply a human performance problem.</p>



<h2>The measurement problem</h2>

<p>Organizations typically judge AI-enabled processes by measures such as <a href="https://www.ibm.com/think/insights/top-5-tips-measuring-productivity-gen-AI-enterprise">accuracy and productivity</a>. Those numbers may look good even as the human role is changing. Suppose employees override AI recommendations less frequently over time. Is that a sign of growing dependence? Perhaps. </p>

<p>But it could also mean that the AI has become more accurate and there is less reason to intervene. The <a href="https://doi.org/10.1613/jair.1.15873">number of overrides alone</a> tells little about whether employees remain ready to exercise their own judgment.</p>

<p>The key is to understand how the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ifacol.2025.09.129">division of work</a> between people and AI is changing. Which decisions have migrated from people to AI? What responsibilities remain with people? Looking at the performance of the employee or the AI separately may miss what is changing between them.</p>

<h2>The governance problem</h2>

<p>Organizational governance – defining roles and responsibilities – is also under pressure from AI.</p>

<p>Someone may remain formally in the loop with an AI system even as their actual role changes. Defining human and AI roles when a system is introduced is only a starting point. As AI improves and people become accustomed to using it, those roles are likely to <a href="https://doi.org/10.5465/amr.2024.0546">change over time</a>. There is nothing inherently wrong with that change. </p>

<p>The problem arises when the relationship changes but the assumptions surrounding it do not. It’s important for organizations to periodically ask: What relationship between people and AI did we design, and what relationship do we actually have today?</p>

<p>In short, organizational governance needs to be dynamic. </p>

<h2>Maintaining the human backstop</h2>

<p>Not every human capability needs to be preserved. If AI can perform a task well, there is little reason to require people to keep doing the same work. Organizations need to decide which capabilities they still expect people to have when human judgment is required. If people may still be called upon to use a capability, it needs to be maintained.</p>

<p>Overseeing AI is not the same as exercising independent judgment. If people rarely make the decision themselves, the organization cannot assume they will be ready when they need to. One way to test this is to occasionally ask employees to make a decision without first seeing the AI recommendation. The organization needs to know that the human backstop it relies on will actually work when needed.</p>

<p>As AI takes on more work, some human capabilities will inevitably be used less often. Some may no longer matter. Others may still be essential when AI reaches its limits. The challenge is knowing the difference and making that choice deliberately.</p>

<p>For me, the central question is this: Which human capabilities does an organization still depend on, and will they be there when needed?</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292340/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
