    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/764992/original/file-20261008-50-7rrhki.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C38%2C6437%2C4291&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">An engraving from 1826 shows a Scottish traveler fighting witches and demons in a church graveyard.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/scottish-traveller-john-o-arnha-fighting-a-kelpy-witches-news-photo/1751366703?phrase=magic%20witches&amp;adppopup=true">Florilegius/Universal Images Group via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Americans who trust science and reason more than their churches’ teachings, but still believe in God or attend services, are also more likely to believe in magic than those who prioritize religious teachings.</p>

<p>This was the central finding of a study my co-authors and <a href="https://www.american.edu/spa/faculty/rli.cfm">I</a> published in the journal <a href="https://doi.org/10.1093/sf/soag097">Social Forces</a> in July 2026. We analyzed the latest wave of the <a href="https://baylorreligionsurvey.research.baylor.edu/">Baylor Religion Survey</a>, a nationally representative survey of 1,812 American adults that <a href="https://www.gallup.com/home.aspx">Gallup</a> fielded in early 2025.</p>

<p>We used four of its questions to measure an outlook we call “secular rationalism.” The term refers to the belief that science is the only way to understand the world and that morality should rest on reason rather than religious teachings. Secular rationalism also includes the idea that people should interpret spiritual matters on their own rather than trust religious authorities.</p>

<p>We looked at people who embrace secular rationalist ideas but also believe in the supernatural. We asked respondents how strongly they believed in six things that people often call magic and require no god or church, from ghosts and curses to talking to the dead. For comparison, we also measured belief in miracles, such as whether miracles still happen today and whether God is the source of all miracles.</p>

<p>What’s interesting was that people who scored high on “secular rationalism” beliefs were more likely to believe in magic, so long as they kept some tie to religion. Among Americans who believe in God, those who also agree with secular rationalism were about twice as likely to lean toward magic as those who reject secular rationalism – 40% vs. 19%. Among people who attend religious services, the share was 28% vs. 19%. Among people who never attend services or do not believe in God, secular rationalism was no longer linked to belief in magic. </p>

<p>Some of the groups we compared were small. According to Baylor Religion Survey 2025 data, fewer than 1% of Americans neither believe in God nor generally agree with these secular rationalist ideas but actively reject them, while about 18% believe in God and agree with them. </p>

<p>Some people may still show up to church, or still believe in God, yet no longer grant their church the authority to define their belief about the supernatural. In short, our research shows, magic thrives where individual rationality and spirituality meet. </p>

<h2>Why it matters</h2>

<p>About 3 in 10 American adults now claim <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2025/02/26/decline-of-christianity-in-the-us-has-slowed-may-have-leveled-off/">no religious affiliation</a>. Scholars are still debating whether the decline of organized religion will also mean the <a href="https://global.oup.com/academic/product/why-religion-went-obsolete-9780197800737?cc=us&amp;lang=en&amp;">decline of belief in the supernatural</a> in the U.S. A long tradition of social theory predicts that as religious institutions decline, a <a href="https://sociology.sas.upenn.edu/sites/default/files/Weber-Science-as-a-Vocation.pdf">scientific outlook with no room</a> for supernatural or magic will take its place. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765893/original/file-20261013-50-d4o76q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Two women seated at a table with a small display sign reading 'Tarot card reading.'" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765893/original/file-20261013-50-d4o76q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765893/original/file-20261013-50-d4o76q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765893/original/file-20261013-50-d4o76q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765893/original/file-20261013-50-d4o76q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765893/original/file-20261013-50-d4o76q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765893/original/file-20261013-50-d4o76q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765893/original/file-20261013-50-d4o76q.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Americans who leave organized religion often retain spiritual beliefs.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/tarot-card-reading-by-yesbelt-as-seen-during-taaf-heritage-news-photo/2276429347?phrase=tarot&amp;adppopup=true">JP Yim/Getty Images for The Asian American Foundation (TAAF)</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Our findings suggest that many Americans who no longer affiliate with an organized religion may still believe in tarot, astrology or psychic services. More broadly, most Americans without a religion still hold some spiritual belief. <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/religion/2025/02/26/religious-and-spiritual-beliefs/">According to the Pew Research Center</a>, 29% of Americans have no religion, but only 5% call themselves atheists. Most say their religion is “nothing in particular,” and two-thirds of that group still believe in something beyond the natural world.</p>

<p>Why are we seeing this trend? As French sociologist Emile Durkheim wrote in 1912, “<a href="https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/41360">The magician has a clientele, not a church</a>.” Magic needs no congregation, clergy or theology, so believers can adopt it without leaving their church. That makes magic a natural fit for people who still believe in God but no longer let institutions define the supernatural for them. It may also explain its appeal to younger Americans, who <a href="https://doi.org/10.1162/daed_a_01943">distrust institutions most</a> and, as our data suggests, are likely to believe in both magic and secular rationalism.</p>

<h2>What’s next</h2>

<p>Our data comes from a single point in time. It shows that people who are religious but also trust science and reason are more likely to believe in magic. But it can’t tell us whether these people are drifting away from religion, coming back to it or staying where they are. To find out, we would need to survey the same people who participated in the original survey over time. </p>

<p>Archaeologist <a href="https://www.arch.ox.ac.uk/people/professor-chris-gosden">Chris Gosden</a> argues that belief in <a href="https://academic.macmillan.com/academictrade/9781250800152/magicahistory/">magic is older</a> than both religion and science, and for most of history it has existed side by side with religion. What our study adds is a clearer picture of when trust in science goes hand in hand with magic: among people who stay religious but no longer let their church decide what is true.</p>

<p>We still know little about how magical beliefs spread among young Americans, or why they appeal to them. Answering those questions is an important next step for research on belief.</p>

<title>Do you think teachers are similar to coaches, pastors or something else? It depends on where you live</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766190/original/file-20261014-50-ozgz4r.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C2%2C6000%2C3999&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">People across the U.S., England and Australia agree that teachers are most like coaches when considering comparable professions. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/happy-black-teacher-and-elementary-student-walking-royalty-free-image/2221704721?phrase=teachers%20and%20student%20relationship&amp;searchscope=image,film&amp;adppopup=true">Drazen Zigic/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Three answers, three countries, one open-ended question: “Teaching is similar to what other occupation or activity?” </p>

<p>We asked this question to more than 3,000 people across the United States, England and Australia between May 2025 and March 2026. </p>

<p>Coaching was the front-runner across all three countries. But the similarities partially diverged there. </p>

<p>Respondents in England and Australia more often compared teaching with professional roles such as nursing and social work. U.S. respondents, meanwhile, more often likened teaching to being a parent and religious roles, such as a cleric or pastor.</p>

<p>In the three countries, however, one other idea stood out: Teaching was primarily associated with a caring relationship. </p>

<p>We have previously <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-makes-a-good-teacher-ask-a-republican-and-a-democrat-and-they-are-likely-to-agree-282130">examined how</a>  Republicans and Democrats in the U.S. find common ground on what makes a good teacher, despite the polarization in the <a href="https://www.carnegiehighered.com/higher-educations-role-in-polarized-america/">country on education</a> and many other issues. </p>

<p>This time, <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=ClEsE9QAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">we wanted</a> <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=STy3ZAEAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">to know</a> <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=dXpvMgIAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">whether people across countries</a> had similar ideas of teachers. </p>

<h2>Common ground</h2>

<p>In all three countries, respondents most often described teaching as centered in the relationship between teacher and student: a form of coaching, caregiving, parenting and other types of personal support. </p>

<p>Coaching was the most common answer in each country, but its prominence varied. </p>

<p>Coaching was named by 30% of U.S. respondents, compared with 23% in England and 23% in Australia. </p>

<p>The differences became more pronounced when participants named other occupations and activities. </p>

<p>Respondents in England and Australia were more likely to associate teaching with institutional, credentialed and paid professional roles, such as nursing, lecturing and social work.</p>

<p>“Nursing. They care for and look after people whilst they are at their most vulnerable. Teachers do a similar thing by caring and teaching young people some of the skills they will need later in life,” a 39-year-old Australian man told us.</p>

<p>“A lecturer, you are passing on knowledge to people, usually the younger generation,” another 32-year-old man in England said. </p>

<p>Compared with respondents in those countries, U.S. respondents were more likely to describe teaching through caregiving roles, such as parenting, and through religious figures, such as priests, pastors or rabbis. </p>

<p>“Being a parent, you are caring for young minds and shaping them through learning,” a 33-year-old woman in the U.S. told us. </p>

<p>“As a preacher, he teaches the word of God. How they deliver the word determines how well the people will understand it,” a 23-year-old woman in the U.S. said. </p>

<p>While international comparisons are informative, they do not represent a single view of teaching. Instead, they suggest that respondents in three countries likely drew on somewhat different cultural repertoires when describing the profession.</p>

<p>We were surprised by just how much agreement we found. </p>

<p>Despite differences in schooling models and cultural norms, people in the United States, England and Australia had remarkably similar ideas about how relationships are at the heart of teaching, closely echoing our other work showing that Republicans and Democrats view teachers similarly. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766192/original/file-20261014-50-9h7a6d.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A man wearing a button down shirt leans on desks while people sitting at the desks face toward him." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766192/original/file-20261014-50-9h7a6d.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766192/original/file-20261014-50-9h7a6d.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766192/original/file-20261014-50-9h7a6d.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766192/original/file-20261014-50-9h7a6d.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766192/original/file-20261014-50-9h7a6d.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766192/original/file-20261014-50-9h7a6d.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766192/original/file-20261014-50-9h7a6d.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">While AI is fueling educational debates, people don’t associate the technology with teachers.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/male-high-school-teacher-and-students-in-classroom-royalty-free-image/103060388?phrase=male%20teachers%20and%20student%20relationship&amp;searchscope=image%2Cfilm&amp;adppopup=true">Connect Images/iStock via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>AI is not at the center of people’s thinking</h2>

<p>In September 2026, <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/28/upshot/ideas-fixing-schools-ranked.html">The New York Times</a> conducted an informal survey of 37 education researchers who gave 30 ideas about how to fix schools. </p>

<p>Their list consists primarily of interventions such as more per-pupil funding,  banning cellphones and restricting artificial intelligence in the classroom. These ideas appeared far less often in our participants’ explanations of what teaching resembles.</p>

<p>In fact, out of more than 3,000 responses to our survey, AI came up only a handful of times and never as the reason teaching and another occupation were said to be alike. </p>

<p>Given how central <a href="https://theconversation.com/we-asked-teachers-about-their-experiences-with-ai-in-the-classroom-heres-what-they-said-265241">AI has become</a> to political and <a href="https://theconversation.com/ai-can-help-with-academic-research-but-doesnt-always-get-it-right-here-are-some-tips-to-check-the-information-you-receive-292865">academic debates</a> about the <a href="https://theconversation.com/when-it-comes-to-developing-policies-on-ai-in-k-12-schools-are-largely-on-their-own-268272">future of education</a>, its near-total absence in these public descriptions of teaching is notable. </p>

<p>At the same time, experts and citizens agree that what separates very good teaching from poor execution is likely the quality of the relationship between educators and children.</p>

<p>We think that serious conversation about student achievement must include clear descriptions of very good teachers: the practices they use to encourage and enable students to learn. Our research shows that teaching should make room for both the transmission of knowledge and the meaningful and caring relationships that make learning possible.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294029/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766284/original/file-20261014-50-ws3vau.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C84%2C1872%2C1248&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Ketamine and many other psychoactive substances can&#39;t be detected by most standard drug screens, so it&#39;s unclear how often they play a role in sexual assault.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/ketamine-bottle-with-warning-label-royalty-free-image/2251150920">D-Keine/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Former Cornell student Jane Doe, who <a href="https://www.cornellsun.com/article/2026/09/tccsuykuvb4z">filed a civil lawsuit in September 2026</a> alleging that seven fraternity members raped her at a party, said the young men who assaulted her pressured her into taking the drug ketamine.  </p>

<p>As an <a href="https://med.virginia.edu/emergency-medicine/faculty/full-time-faculty/christopher-p-holstege-md/">emergency room physician, medical toxicologist</a> and the <a href="https://studentaffairs.virginia.edu/staff/christopher-holstege">head of student health services</a> at the University of Virginia, I have had a front-row seat to the growing danger that psychoactive substances such as ketamine present to the health and safety of university students. </p>

<p><a href="https://med.virginia.edu/toxicology/wp-content/uploads/sites/268/2026/03/Mar26-Ketamine-analogues.pdf">Ketamine and its emerging spin-off versions</a> are part of a <a href="https://www.unodc.org/unodc/secured/wdr/wdr2013/World_Drug_Report_2013.pdf">wave of new and evolving designer drugs</a> entering the United States and other countries. How widely these substances are used remains unknown, since most hospitals are <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.emc.2022.01.003">unable to detect them</a> on standard urine drug screens. But <a href="https://www.justice.gov/archive/ndic/pubs8/8872/index.htm#commission">ketamine and other drugs</a> are being increasingly reported as <a href="https://doi.org/10.28933/ijprr-2021-07-1505">agents used in sexual assault</a> – either when people take these drugs voluntarily, are pressured to take them or are given them covertly. </p>

<p>The increasing prevalence of ketamine and other drugs – and their use in sexual assault – is <a href="https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.focus.20180037">playing out on college campuses across the U.S.</a> and putting students at risk. </p>



<h2>A growing supply</h2>

<p>Ketamine is a synthetic chemical that was <a href="https://www.ebsco.com/research-starters/health-and-medicine/ketamine/">first synthesized in 1962</a>. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved it as a <a href="https://doi.org/10.3389/fnhum.2016.00612">general anesthetic for people and animals</a> in 1970, and doctors and veterinarians used it for decades to induce anesthesia during surgeries and to relieve pain. </p>

<p>People have <a href="https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.books.9798894551944.lg03">used ketamine recreationally</a> since the 1970s. Getting high on it became more popular in the U.S. in the 1980s, when it was called “Special K.” It was frequently found in the club drug scenes and was associated with raves into the 1990s. Today, ketamine is sold on the street under a <a href="https://www.justice.gov/archive/ndic/pubs8/8872/8872p.pdf">variety of slang names</a>, such as K, Ket, and Vitamin K. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766291/original/file-20261014-50-ozw15y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="An outdoor college party with strobe lights, and palm trees in the background." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766291/original/file-20261014-50-ozw15y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766291/original/file-20261014-50-ozw15y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766291/original/file-20261014-50-ozw15y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766291/original/file-20261014-50-ozw15y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766291/original/file-20261014-50-ozw15y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766291/original/file-20261014-50-ozw15y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766291/original/file-20261014-50-ozw15y.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">The prevalence of ketamine and other psychoactive drugs in the U.S., including on college campuses, has spiked since the early 2010s.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/outdoor-college-party-royalty-free-image/1751137399">Jeremy Bernfeld/iStock via Getty Images Plus</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In 2019, <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S2045796019000751">the FDA approved a nasal spray version of ketamine</a>, called esketamine, to treat depression that does not respond to other treatments. That drug’s use is tightly regulated, but clinicians are increasingly prescribing ketamine “off-label” for a variety of psychiatric conditions, including <a href="https://theconversation.com/ketamine-can-rapidly-reduce-symptoms-of-ptsd-and-depression-new-study-finds-216077">post-traumatic stress disorder</a>. </p>

<p>Cases of poisoning caused by ketamine in the U.S. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.drugalcdep.2025.112549">doubled between 2019 and 2023</a>, according to an analysis of calls to poison control centers nationwide, and are now the highest they’ve ever been. This surge is in part due to the more widespread medical use of ketamine, which makes accessing it much easier. But <a href="https://doi.org/10.1001/jamapsychiatry.2023.1423">street versions of the drug</a> are also prevalent as chemists in basement laboratories create novel ketamine analogs.  </p>

<h2>Ketamine’s effects on the body</h2>

<p>Ketamine’s effects vary depending on the dose and the person. It can cause someone to dissociate, creating an altered state of consciousness, changing what’s perceived through the senses and causing a sense of detachment from one’s self and one’s surroundings. The drug can also <a href="https://www.merckmanuals.com/professional/special-subjects/illicit-drugs-and-intoxicants/ketamine-and-phencyclidine">cause coma at high doses</a>. </p>

<p>Someone who orally consumes ketamine would typically begin to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/20961790.2017.1285219">feel its effects within 20 minutes</a>. If they inhale or inject it, the effects are almost immediate. The primary effects generally wear off in less than an hour, but a person’s senses may remain dulled and their judgment and coordination impaired for several hours afterward. </p>

<p>Ketamine can cause a slew of other side effects, including delirium, amnesia, increased salivation, abnormal eye movements, high blood pressure and potentially fatal breathing problems. Alcohol and other drugs can <a href="https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms23147800">interact with ketamine to worsen these effects</a> significantly. </p>

<p>Ketamine is generally sold illegally as either a colorless, odorless liquid or a white or off-white powder. Either form can be easily and covertly placed into an unsuspecting person’s beverage or food. Ketamine can be snorted, and it can be smoked or vaped on products such as marijuana. </p>

<h2>Ketamine and other drugs in sexual assault</h2>

<p>Research is extremely spotty on how often a perpetrator of rape or sexual assault <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.emc.2007.02.008">uses a chemical agent</a> – whether ketamine, alcohol or another substance – to alter a victim’s senses. Research suggests that most often both parties <a href="https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/108860">use mind-altering substances voluntarily</a>, although the effects of these substances can alter a person’s ability to grant consent. </p>

<p>Even so, there are numerous reports of perpetrators spiking a victim’s drink or otherwise slipping a drug to them without their knowledge. According to one study, <a href="https://www.ojp.gov/library/publications/estimate-incidence-drug-facilitated-sexual-assault-us-final-report">4.2% of rape victims were drugged covertly</a>, though how often this actually happens is undoubtedly underreported. </p>

<p>That’s because it’s very hard to detect drugs taken this way. Most of the substances used to facilitate sexual assaults are rapidly absorbed and metabolized by the body, rendering them difficult to detect in routine urine and blood drug screenings. Another issue is that many days may have elapsed between the victim ingesting the drugs and their subsequent treatment at a medical facility. </p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/DcvNyuZ6KVk?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Ketamine’s increasing use in the clinic has helped fuel its popularity as a party drug.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Victims of rape or sexual assault are often reluctant to report incidents because of a sense of embarrassment, guilt or perceived responsibility, or because they may know their attacker. Some may <a href="https://theconversation.com/handling-of-rape-allegations-at-cornell-shows-why-so-many-assaults-go-unreported-victims-dont-trust-the-institutions-that-are-supposed-to-help-them-293907">not trust that their institution or local law enforcement</a> will support them.</p>

<p>In my experience, the involvement of ketamine or other drugs invariably makes a bad situation worse – complicating consent, impairing judgment and reducing inhibitions. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1016/j.emc.2007.02.008">Ketamine causes confusion and drowsiness</a>, and its sedative, hypnotic and memory-erasing properties can diminish a survivor’s recollection of events surrounding the sexual assault. </p>

<p>The availability of these drugs in the U.S., including on college campuses, has risen sharply – particularly since the early 2010s, as a slew of new substances have emerged and <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/bcp.14236">international drug control efforts have not kept up</a>. Without more active education and prevention efforts, as well as better detection methods for these drugs, students will continue to pay the price.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293512/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Why the GOP’s voter fraud messaging may backfire</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765661/original/file-20261012-50-ioww4h.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C6700%2C4466&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">A sticker on a lamppost warns of voter fraud on Nov. 7, 2022, in Anchorage, Alaska. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/sticker-on-a-lamp-post-warns-of-voter-fraud-on-november-07-news-photo/1244593156?phrase=voter%20fraud&amp;adppopup=true">Spencer Platt/Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>With Election Day 2026 just weeks away and control of Congress hanging in the balance, the results will almost certainly hinge on voter turnout, <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/feature/how-changes-in-turnout-and-vote-choice-powered-trumps-victory-in-2024/">just as they did</a> in 2024.</p>

<p>Given that genuinely undecided voters are scarce — <a href="https://www.nbcnews.com/politics/2026-election/16-undecided-voters-are-weighing-2026-election-options-rcna599899">as little as 5%</a> to <a href="https://thehill.com/homenews/campaign/6105250-voters-america-wrong-direction-midterms-poll/">7% of the electorate</a>, according to major polls — both Democrats and Republicans must look to mobilize their rank-and-file supporters. To do so, the Republican Party has bet strongly this year on <a href="https://revealnews.org/podcast/voter-fraud-christian-adams-elections-rights/">a strategy of convincing people</a> that <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/04/07/us/politics/trump-mail-voting-elections-fact-check.html">voter fraud is rampant</a>. </p>

<p><a href="https://polisci.richmond.edu/faculty/cmiller3/">As a scholar of U.S. politics</a>, I see this as a high-risk strategy for Republican candidates and American democracy. That’s because reduced trust in election integrity can <a href="https://statesunited.org/resources/when-americans-trust-elections/">reduce motivation to vote</a> – even if based on flawed information. But it’s not at all clear which Americans are most likely to stay home in November.</p>

<h2>Voter fraud vs. reality</h2>

<p><a href="https://www.americanbar.org/groups/crsj/resources/human-rights/2026-september/debunking-voter-fraud-myth-again/">Voter fraud is not a real problem</a> in the United States. Study after study, by <a href="https://www.senatoredmcbroom.com/senate-oversight-committee-releases-report-on-november-2020-general-election/">public officials</a> and <a href="https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/analysis-opinion/analysis-heritage-foundations-database-undermines-claims-recent-voter">think tanks</a>, has shown that <a href="https://www.cato.org/testimony/restoring-election-integrity-oversight-voter-fraud-new-jersey#">voting by noncitizens and other ineligible voters</a> happens only at minuscule, statistically insignificant levels. </p>

<p>Nonetheless, <a href="https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/americans-increased-belief-voter-fraud-180029721.html">rhetoric from the Trump administration</a> about voter fraud has been pervasive. Consider the recent claim by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin that <a href="https://www.dhs.gov/news/2026/07/17/dhs-secretary-markwayne-mullin-sends-letters-secretaries-state-warning-about-non">Nevada had nearly 16,000 noncitizens</a> on its voter rolls – a number reduced to 185 when state authorities pressed for details, and <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/24/us/politics/nevada-voters-homeland-security-trump.html">reduced to zero</a> when the state investigated the names provided. </p>

<p>There is comparable behavior from Congress. <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/27671127.2025.2478863">My own research</a> on political communication has shown that a substantial number of members of Congress, strongly skewing Republican, make frequent use of rhetoric that undermines democratic norms and delegitimizes political institutions.</p>

<p>The strategy ties readily into President Donald Trump’s <a href="https://www.propublica.org/article/big-lie-trump-stolen-election-inside-creation">persistent false claims that he won the 2020 presidential election</a>. It also ties into his <a href="https://www.whitehouse.gov/releases/2026/02/americans-overwhelmingly-support-deporting-criminal-illegals-local-cooperation-with-ice/">administration’s strongly anti-immigrant agenda</a>, which spreads fear of <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/1-in-3-fears-immigrants-influence-us-elections-ap-norc-poll">noncitizens corrupting U.S. politics</a>.  </p>

<p>How does this uncertain political environment influence voters? </p>

<p>There is <a href="https://yankelovichcenter.ucsd.edu/public-engagement/CTTE-Report-2025-2026_2.17.pdf">clear data showing</a> that voter confidence in elections has fallen across party lines: Only 65% of Republicans, 64% of Democrats and 57% of independent voters are very or somewhat confident that the 2026 vote count will be reliable. <a href="https://statesunited.org/resources/when-americans-trust-elections/">Conventional wisdom suggests</a> such discouraging numbers would depress turnout.</p>

<p>It’s not as simple as that, however. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765662/original/file-20261012-50-iupqva.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A person in a crowd indoors holds a white sign with the words 'No Voter Fraud' on it." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765662/original/file-20261012-50-iupqva.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/765662/original/file-20261012-50-iupqva.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765662/original/file-20261012-50-iupqva.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765662/original/file-20261012-50-iupqva.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765662/original/file-20261012-50-iupqva.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765662/original/file-20261012-50-iupqva.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/765662/original/file-20261012-50-iupqva.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A ‘no voter fraud’ sign is displayed in support of President Donald Trump at the Maricopa County Elections Department office on Nov. 4, 2020, in Phoenix.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/no-voter-fraud-sign-is-displayed-by-a-protester-in-support-news-photo/1229466917?phrase=voter%20fraud&amp;adppopup=true">Courtney Pedroza/Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>What motivates voters</h2>

<p>Extensive research confirms the axiom that a sense of civic duty is the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s11109-018-9459-3">strongest predictor of whether someone will vote</a>. It supersedes trust, partisanship and policy preferences.</p>

<p>Any campaign’s quest to mobilize additional voters, therefore, must find them among citizens without a strong sense of civic duty. But among these people, diminished trust in democratic processes can play out in counterintuitive ways. </p>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1057/s41269-026-00442-9">Recent research on German voters</a> is relevant to the U.S.: It shows that among more passive voters – those following cues from political elites – reduced trust in elections can depress motivation to vote. That’s because there’s no trustworthy result that voters are seeking to affirm. </p>

<p>Conversely, among voters with greater skepticism about elite messaging, reduced trust can motivate increased turnout as an attempted corrective for a flawed system. </p>

<p>What does this mean for potential voters in the U.S.? Among Republicans, it appears that the party’s strategy carries a strong risk of backlash. </p>

<p><a href="https://electionlab.mit.edu/sites/default/files/2023-10/voter-trust.pdf">Findings from MIT’s Election Lab</a> confirm that cues from political elites are a powerful factor in voter behavior. Specifically, cues setting expectations of a disappointing or untrustworthy result will reduce motivation. Why vote if you don’t expect it to help achieve the desired result? </p>

<p>The same study finds Republican voters broadly inclined to believe GOP leaders’ cues about voter fraud and to frame their expectations accordingly. And once they’ve made that shift, they <a href="https://electionlab.mit.edu/sites/default/files/2023-10/voter-trust.pdf">cling firmly to the belief</a>, even in the face of contrary empirical evidence or messaging from within the party. </p>

<p>In the current election cycle, 50% of <a href="https://yankelovichcenter.ucsd.edu/public-engagement/CTTE-Report-2025-2026_2.17.pdf">Republicans surveyed</a> distrust mail-in voting, and 51% fear voting by noncitizens. They expect election results to be fraudulent. This likely won’t mobilize them, as there’s no positive result they can expect to affirm. The Republican Party’s messaging has painted its voters into a corner.</p>

<p>Democrats, meanwhile, are less inclined to believe claims of voter fraud. But they are <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/09/10/us/politics/department-of-justice-election-fraud-states.html">more inclined to be concerned</a> about attempts to undermine the midterms by political elites making such claims. Examples include the Trump administration’s efforts to sow doubt about <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-the-supreme-court-blocked-trump-and-the-postal-service-from-restricting-mail-in-voting-for-the-midterms-291319">voting by mail</a> and about alleged <a href="https://www.npr.org/2026/09/25/nx-s1-5976804/supreme-court-trump-save-noncitizen-voting">noncitizen voting</a>.</p>

<p>These efforts increase motivation to vote among Democrats. Unlike GOP voters, they see the capacity to correct for the system’s vulnerabilities – the potential and urgency to overwhelm attempts at voter suppression through higher turnout.</p>

<h2>Truth and trust</h2>

<p>Opponents of Trump and the GOP may find these diverging effects encouraging. No matter the results this November, however, we’re left with a precarious dynamic. Increasing numbers of voters lack trust in elections and make their decisions to vote – or not – based on limited or flawed information. </p>

<p>Fortunately, there are signs of hope. </p>

<p>Although voters in general <a href="https://electionlab.mit.edu/sites/default/files/2023-10/voter-trust.pdf">are poorly informed</a> about how elections are conducted, they can and do respond <a href="https://theconversation.com/election-officials-are-fighting-wavering-voter-trust-by-making-mundane-processes-visible-and-recruiting-citizens-to-help-292199">to clear information</a> familiarizing them with election processes. </p>

<p>I’ve seen this myself over the years, working with nonpartisan efforts to register young adults and train them as poll watchers. And in the current election cycle, there have already been <a href="https://protectdemocracy.org/work/frequently-asked-questions-about-the-2026-midterm-elections/">widespread efforts</a> to <a href="https://karshinstitute.virginia.edu/news/emergency-powers-and-elections-whats-stake-2026">broaden public awareness</a> about the fact that state officials, not federal ones, <a href="https://statedemocracy.law.wisc.edu/our-work/can-the-federal-government-force-states-to-hand-over-citizens-voter-information">have authority over voter rolls</a> and election security. </p>

<p>Meanwhile, <a href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/voters-trust-local-election-officials-theyre-less-sure-about-the-mail">fewer Americans are expected to vote by mail this year</a> – whether due to fear of fraud or <a href="https://www.lwv.org/newsroom/news-clips/postmaster-generals-remarks-mail-ballots-stoke-fears-among-voting-rights">fear of the Post Office</a>. If they instead vote in person, a silver lining is that positive <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/1065912908324870">personal experiences with poll workers</a> are also associated with increased voter trust. </p>

<p>Looking beyond November, what Americans can hope for is a cycle in which clear election outcomes provide an opportunity to inform voters of how and why the system works. That’s the way to motivate more political engagement and voter turnout in the future.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292106/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

body: A sticker on a lamppost warns of voter fraud on Nov. 7, 2022, in Anchorage, Alaska
Spencer Platt/Getty Images With Election Day 2026 just weeks away and control of Congress hanging in the balance, the results will almost certainly hinge on voter turnout, just as they did in 2024

Given that genuinely undecided voters are scarce — as little as 5% to 7% of the electorate , according to major polls — both Democrats and Republicans must look to mobilize their rank-and-file supporters
To do so, the Republican Party has bet strongly this year on a strategy of convincing people that voter fraud is rampant
As a scholar of U.S. politics , I see this as a high-risk strategy for Republican candidates and American democracy
That’s because reduced trust in election integrity can reduce motivation to vote – even if based on flawed information
But it’s not at all clear which Americans are most likely to stay home in November
Voter fraud vs. reality Voter fraud is not a real problem in the United States
Study after study, by public officials and think tanks , has shown that voting by noncitizens and other ineligible voters happens only at minuscule, statistically insignificant levels
Nonetheless, rhetoric from the Trump administration about voter fraud has been pervasive

Consider the recent claim by Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin that Nevada had nearly 16,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls – a number reduced to 185 when state authorities pressed for details, and reduced to zero when the state investigated the names provided
There is comparable behavior from Congress

My own research on political communication has shown that a substantial number of members of Congress, strongly skewing Republican, make frequent use of rhetoric that undermines democratic norms and delegitimizes political institutions
The strategy ties readily into President Donald Trump’s persistent false claims that he won the 2020 presidential election
It also ties into his administration’s strongly anti-immigrant agenda , which spreads fear of noncitizens corrupting U.S. politics

How does this uncertain political environment influence voters? There is clear data showing that voter confidence in elections has fallen across party lines: Only 65% of Republicans, 64% of Democrats and 57% of independent voters are very or somewhat confident that the 2026 vote count will be reliable
Conventional wisdom suggests such discouraging numbers would depress turnout
A ‘no voter fraud’ sign is displayed in support of President Donald Trump at the Maricopa County Elections Department office on Nov. 4, 2020, in Phoenix
Courtney Pedroza/Getty Images What motivates voters Extensive research confirms the axiom that a sense of civic duty is the strongest predictor of whether someone will vote
It supersedes trust, partisanship and policy preferences
Any campaign’s quest to mobilize additional voters, therefore, must find them among citizens without a strong sense of civic duty
But among these people, diminished trust in democratic processes can play out in counterintuitive ways

Recent research on German voters is relevant to the U.S.: It shows that among more passive voters – those following cues from political elites – reduced trust in elections can depress motivation to vote
That’s because there’s no trustworthy result that voters are seeking to affirm
Conversely, among voters with greater skepticism about elite messaging, reduced trust can motivate increased turnout as an attempted corrective for a flawed system
What does this mean for potential voters in the U.S.? Among Republicans, it appears that the party’s strategy carries a strong risk of backlash
Findings from MIT’s Election Lab confirm that cues from political elites are a powerful factor in voter behavior
Specifically, cues setting expectations of a disappointing or untrustworthy result will reduce motivation

Why vote if you don’t expect it to help achieve the desired result? The same study finds Republican voters broadly inclined to believe GOP leaders’ cues about voter fraud and to frame their expectations accordingly
And once they’ve made that shift, they cling firmly to the belief , even in the face of contrary empirical evidence or messaging from within the party
In the current election cycle, 50% of Republicans surveyed distrust mail-in voting, and 51% fear voting by noncitizens
They expect election results to be fraudulent
This likely won’t mobilize them, as there’s no positive result they can expect to affirm
The Republican Party’s messaging has painted its voters into a corner
Democrats, meanwhile, are less inclined to believe claims of voter fraud
But they are more inclined to be concerned about attempts to undermine the midterms by political elites making such claims
Examples include the Trump administration’s efforts to sow doubt about voting by mail and about alleged noncitizen voting
These efforts increase motivation to vote among Democrats
Unlike GOP voters, they see the capacity to correct for the system’s vulnerabilities – the potential and urgency to overwhelm attempts at voter suppression through higher turnout

title: Trump’s plan to deport a member of Congress
excerpt: Ilhan Omar (D-MN) during a news conference at the US Capitol on February 24, 2026. | Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images This story appeared in  The Lo
body: Ilhan Omar (D-MN) during a news conference at the US Capitol on February 24, 2026. | Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here
Welcome to The Logoff: Donald Trump wants to deport a member of Congress.  What’s happening? On Monday, Homeland Security officers raided the Washington, DC, home of US Rep
Ilhan Omar (D-MN) in an investigation reportedly tied to immigration paperwork filled out by her father when she was a minor
That was, at the time, more than enough cause for alarm

Trump’s animosity toward Omar , who is Somali-American and an outspoken critic of the administration, is well-known, and the raid is an extraordinary violation of the Justice Department’s usual rule to avoid taking visible action around politically sensitive cases within 60 days of an election.  On Wednesday evening, however, we learned more about the raid from the Wall Street Journal

The Omar investigation, the Journal reported, is explicitly aimed at stripping Omar of her citizenship — and thus her ability to hold office — and deporting her.  How would they do that? Omar came to the US as a refugee when she was 12 and became a US citizen when she was 17

The Trump administration’s investigation is said to focus on whether she or her family misrecorded her age in order to more easily gain citizenship.  The government cannot unilaterally denaturalize a citizen, however; it would have to ask a court to do so
What’s the context? Historically, it’s rare for the US to strip citizenship from naturalized US citizens

But doing so at volume has been a major, if less visible, priority for the second Trump administration.  As of earlier this year, NBC News reported , DOJ was targeting hundreds of people for possible denaturalization, and has reportedly hoped to put forward hundreds of new cases per month (though successfully stripping them of citizenship is another matter)

Why does this matter? Trump’s campaign to bend the traditionally nonpartisan DOJ into a tool to punish and harass his enemies has been one of the major stories of his second term.  Even if it never advances beyond Monday’s raid, an investigation targeting Omar’s citizenship with the eventual goal of deporting her from the US represents a new and even more dangerous evolution of that effort — and it threatens to move the US to a far darker place, where citizenship and the rights it guarantees are predicated on the president’s goodwill
And with that, it’s time to log off… Hi readers — if you’ll allow me to depart a little from my normal approach to this section, I have a story about politics to share
It’s not, however, about the politics we’re currently dealing with, but about what could be: Democrats’ plan for a quietly ambitious “Project 2029” should they win the White House in 2028
Alternatively, if you’d prefer to just log off, here’s an adorable snow leopard cub with massive paws
Thanks for reading, have a great evening, and we’ll see you tomorrow!

title: Cold weather and high prices could flip the Senate
excerpt: Susan Collins is behind in one poll by just 2 points as the midterm campaign enters its home stretch. | Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call This story appeared in Today, Ex
body: Susan Collins is behind in one poll by just 2 points as the midterm campaign enters its home stretch. | Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call This story appeared in Today, Explained, a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day

Throughout his second term, President Donald Trump has saddled his party with no shortage of political liabilities — from the mass pardons of January 6 convictions to ICE killings of US citizens to questionable Reflecting Pool redesign choices
For voters, however, there is one stain on Trump’s record more unsightly than all the rest: his failure to reduce Americans’ cost of living
As the midterm campaign enters its home stretch, Americans’ expenses are rising — and the GOP’s prospects are consequently dimming
Last month, consumer prices were 3.7 percent higher than they had been one year earlier, according to a Consumer Price Index report released on Wednesday
That represented an acceleration in the inflation rate, one driven largely by skyrocketing fuel prices: Gasoline was 9.1 percent more expensive in September than it had been in August
As a result, America’s average real wage has fallen by 44 cents since January
In less than three weeks, Americans will head to the polls to decide which party controls Congress, along with a slew of state and local offices

As we count down to that momentous and potentially messy day, this newsletter is partnering with our colleague Astead Herndon and Vox’s The Midterms, Actually team for weekly editions on the biggest issues shaping the midterms
We’re breaking down one issue each week and suggesting further reading and races to watch in November
Last week, we tackled the data center backlash
And this week, we’re digging into affordability
Go a little deeper View Link These upward trends in prices aren’t lost on voters
In a recent Pew Research survey , just 21 percent of Americans said economic conditions were “excellent” or “good” — while 65 percent said that Trump’s policies had made the economy worse
The high cost of living is weighing on Republican candidates in all battleground races
Maine provides just one example of how potent the issue could prove on Election Day
From one angle, the state’s Senate race might seem like a gimme for Democrats
Kamala Harris won Maine by nearly 7 points in 2024
Thus, in 2026 — when Democrats are poised to win in a national landslide — one might expect the party to easily triumph
But Republican incumbent Susan Collins is an unusually formidable foe
The race has been a dead heat, with Democratic nominee Troy Jackson leading by just 2 points in a recent Suffolk University poll

Fortunately for Jackson, Mainers’ energy bills are expected to soar in the campaign’s final weeks, plausibly increasing voters’ appetite for change in the process.  Maine is America’s second coldest state and unusually reliant on oil for home heat
As autumn advances, its residents will use more heating oil, thereby driving up both their personal bills and market prices
Thanks to the global energy crunch, a gallon of such fuel is already nearly twice as expensive as it was this time last year
Jackson has been hitting Collins on the issue relentlessly

That could put a chill in Collins’s reelection odds — and thus, the GOP’s hopes of retaining Senate control. ➨ Other races to watch: Similar dynamics are playing out in perennially icy Alaska, where Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola has hammered incumbent Republican Dan Sullivan for his complicity in sky-high diesel prices , which many Alaskans use for home heat
In Ohio’s Senate race, Democrat Sherrod Brown has tried to pin rising electricity bills on Republican Sen
Jon Husted, due to his support for data center development

And in Texas, Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico has attacked his Republican rival, state Attorney General Ken Paxton, for supporting “this disastrous war in Iran that’s driving up our costs.” In other news A brief ceasefire ends: Ukrainian drones attacked a Russian oil refinery early Thursday, days after Trump demanded both Russia and Ukraine halt such attacks
Execution livestream canceled: Trump canceled a plan to livestream the execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Malik Hasan by firing squad
On the podcast: A recent rash of violence between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis threatens to destabilize the region — and make the Iran war much larger
Research shows confidence is good for your job and good for your romantic prospects
Unsurprisingly, then, a whole industry has sprung up teaching people to be more confident
One writer signed up to work with a confidence coach for the first time, and ended up doubting that her self-doubt was all that bad

Before you go… Did you know… there are four state laws regarding real estate and paranormal activity in the US ? That’s because purported hauntings are just one of many factors that can affect home prices
