Look for the answer in tomorrow’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: We asked which percussion instrument is famously played by Mississippi State University fans at home football games

title: Why your health insurance is dropping GLP-1 coverage
excerpt: The promise of GLP-1 drugs has always depended on people being able to afford them
body: The promise of GLP-1 drugs has always depended on people being able to afford them

These drugs still cost hundreds of dollars per month if you’re paying cash, at which point access becomes a privilege: The higher-income executive who wants to trim a few pounds might be able to afford them either way, but the low-income worker who needs the drug to lose significant weight might not be able to afford them — unless their health insurance covers it
For a while, the trend lines for GLP-1 insurance coverage were positive
As of 2026, roughly two-thirds of private employer plans, which insure half of Americans, were covering GLP-1 medications for weight loss to treat obesity
Over the summer, Medicare launched a new $50-per-month prescription program
The US has struggled with an obesity epidemic for decades, but it looked like powerful drugs to treat it were finally starting to be more seamlessly integrated into the health system
At least that’s how things appeared earlier this year
But now, private plans are pulling back from GLP-1 coverage
People are being left in the lurch, debating whether to try to pay for these drugs on their own or stop taking medicines they feel are making a real difference for their health
The dilemma reveals one of the structural flaws in American healthcare
For working-age adults, your insurance depends on your job

Unfortunately, because people no longer stay at the same job for decades, there is not a strong financial incentive for employers to make investments that will benefit your health in the long term — but there is a strong incentive to minimize short-term costs as much as possible

It’s the kind of perverse rationale that could compel employer-sponsored health plans to stop covering a drug that, if taken over the full course of a person’s life, could help them not only lose weight but ultimately reduce their risk of heart disease, kidney disease and other chronic health problems , improving their health and saving all of us money as they get older. “An employer or an insurer making coverage decisions doesn’t necessarily care if they’re saving Medicare money,” said Dan Sacks , a healthcare economist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. “That’s a classic problem with the American health insurance system, and it’s certainly salient here.” This mismatch between what’s good for people’s health and what’s good for the corporate bottom line has long been one of the underlying flaws in the US health system
Now access to GLP-1 drugs is shrinking just as these drugs were starting to make a real dent in the US obesity crisis

Why employer-sponsored health plans are suddenly dropping GLP-1 coverage From the beginning , insurance coverage was the big question hanging over GLP-1s and their potential to revolutionize US healthcare
But recently, it looked like we’d turned a corner
When I attended the Aspen Ideas: Health festival over the summer, pharmaceutical reps seemed visibly relieved that GLP-1 coverage had been picking up among private insurers

In 2026, about two out of every three employer-sponsored plans were covering some of these drugs for weight management, up from about 20 percent just the year before. “They’re recognizing that this is an investment in their workforce,” said Laura Steele, who leads the cardiometabolic health unit at Eli Lilly, which manufactures Zepbound and Foundayo. “Yes, there is a budget, and there is a benefit design that every employer has

But they’re also recognizing the overall cost that they’re experiencing by not dealing with this too.” But as employers and private insurers make coverage decisions for next year, they are suddenly pulling back

At least 10 percent of employer plans that currently cover GLP-1s for weight loss say they are likely to discontinue coverage in 2027, according to one survey by the Business Group on Health — and that number may still increase
A Mercer survey of large employers found that 6 percent had dropped coverage in 2026 and another 5 percent were planning to in 2027 or actively considering it

A separate report from the Health Policy Commission in Massachusetts found that the number of commercially insured people in the state taking a GLP-1 drug had fallen by 50 percent between 2025 and the first quarter of 2026 as private coverage started to drop off.  Some of the biggest brands in the US are reportedly eliminating or reducing their coverage: PepsiCo , Starbucks , and Lowe’s among them
And their reasons are simple: It’s too expensive
The drugs still carry a high net price tag — $600 or more for a 30-day supply — and potential demand is high ( two in every five American adults have obesity)
When a lot of people start taking an expensive medication all at once, it’s going to raise costs for employer insurance plans — and they have to figure out how to adapt
Insurers set premiums at the start of each year, based on how many people are on the plan and how much healthcare they are expected to need

But if those estimates are off — say, if more people take an expensive GLP-1 drug than the insurer expected — they have to offset those costs somehow, and raising premiums the following year is a common solution
According to one estimate, premiums are projected to grow by 5 to 13 percent due to GLP-1 costs — and the burden of paying those higher premiums is likely to fall on the workers

The employer can also try to limit GLP-1 use by, for example, asking workers to pay more out of pocket for these drugs; according to Mercer , 27 percent of large US employers instituted some kind of utilization controls for GLP-1 drugs over the past year or plan to next year
They also have the option to simply stop covering these drugs for weight loss altogether — and that’s the route more and more of them are deciding to take

The abrupt reversal has even caught economists like Sacks off guard. 3 big reasons employer health plans are dropping GLP-1 coverage Employers aren’t invested in people’s long-term health: As Americans switch jobs more often, companies want to cut short-term costs
GLP-1 prices are still high, upward of $600 per month per person for insurers

A lot of people are eligible to take them for weight loss; two in five US adults have obesity. “I was surprised that anyone would do an about-face because I thought they understood the trade-offs well,” Sacks said. “My guess is that it turned out to be more expensive than they anticipated: Take-up is higher, and possibly more people are sticking with it

That’s one reason that you might not want to continue to offer it.” For employers, the short-term costs of covering a drug often outweigh the long-term benefits that medication may confer, at least from the employer’s POV

One analysis — notably produced by Blue Cross Blue Shield Kansas — concluded that covering GLP-1s for weight loss increased average employee health costs by $7,000 in the first year and another $4,200 in the second, largely due to the cost of the drugs themselves
And yet at the same time, there were no decreases in obesity-related medical events in that time period
Another study from Sacks and his colleagues at Indiana University and the University of South Carolina found that GLP-1 use did not lead to any cost savings over five years

So in the short term, these employers are arguably making an economically rational decision — but one that may still come at their employees’ expense. “I’m completely screwed,” said one person on Reddit about Cigna’s plans to drop GLP-1 coverage for their own employees

They’re looking at at least $300 for one month’s supply at cash prices.  They weren’t alone either: “I’m devastated,” said another person, commenting on Starbucks’s decision to stop covering GLP-1 drugs
They said they had an autoimmune condition that had made it difficult to lose weight — until this new class of medicines came along

title: Why even a Democratic wave might not stop Trump
excerpt: President Donald Trump speaks on stage at the Butler-Vandalia Student Activity Center during a campaign rally on October 3, 2026, in Vandalia, Ohio. | Roberto S
body: President Donald Trump speaks on stage at the Butler-Vandalia Student Activity Center during a campaign rally on October 3, 2026, in Vandalia, Ohio. | Roberto Schmidt/Getty Images Welcome to The Midterms, Actually
Every week I’ll be writing about two things: one big idea or trend I see forming across the 2026 primaries, and one thing I’m hearing from a voice on the ground

One big idea: How much can Democrats slow down Trump? A tricky thing to communicate about the upcoming midterms is that, at the federal level, the impact may not be what’s expected, at least when it comes to slowing President Donald Trump’s agenda
Say the blue wave predicted by most polling materializes on November 3, and Democrats take the House and even squeak out a slim Senate majority
What happens next? Does that stop Trump from executing his agenda? Does the White House moderate its message in response to an electoral backlash? The evidence suggests no
Because the backlash is real, the political incentives aren’t
Let me explain: The numbers do look rough for Trump
Pew had his approval rating at 30 percent in a survey conducted September 28 to October 4, the lowest of his second term, with Democrats up eight on the generic House ballot
Reuters/Ipsos had him at 32 percent in early October
Polling averages are a bit higher, roughly 37 percent to 39 percent depending on the aggregator
Ballotpedia’s September average put Democrats at 50 percent on the generic ballot to Republicans’ 43 percent
Trump is fundamentally shameless, untethered to traditional political incentives, and increasingly unhinged in his second term
He initiated a war with Iran that quite literally no one wanted
He’s plowing ahead with renewed mass deportation efforts even as Republicans urge him to abort the mission
He’s more unpopular by the month, and more consumed by vanity projects in Washington: the White House ballroom, a federal takeover of a DC golf course, whatever’s happening at the reflecting pool
More importantly, he’s been quietly preparing for this moment of backlash, legally and politically
If there’s one theme of Trump’s second term, beyond the promises of retribution, it’s his drive to grow executive power to the point where he’s insulated from political consequences
Let ’ s run the tape The legacy of Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency was less about finding waste, fraud, and abuse than about asserting presidential power over the federal bureaucracy
Trump has brought independent agencies to heel, firing members of the National Labor Relations Board and the Federal Trade Commission

Slaughter , the Supreme Court sided with him 6-3, overturning the 90-year-old Humphrey’s Executor precedent that had limited when presidents could remove agency heads. (The one notable exception: The Court refused, 5-4, to let him remove Fed governor Lisa Cook for now.) His immigration push included federalizing National Guard troops for domestic purposes
He’s pursued unilateral military action that breaks precedent, like the Caribbean boat strikes on suspected drug smugglers

And he’s picked another fight with Congress that’s headed to court, unilaterally withholding roughly $800 million in congressionally approved funds from 11 programs supporting refugees and asylum-seekers, minority business development, housing counseling, and more
To be clear, I don’t believe this anti-democratic throughline is happenstance

Trump has systematically used his first two years back in office to grow the power of the presidency and find ways to execute his agenda without Congress, as he did with his many tariffs — which he also claims, wrongly, that he can use to personally authorize $5,000 checks

His MAGA base has always believed the ends justify the means, but this White House has gone a step further, making clear it won’t be constrained by pesky things like federal law, separation of powers, and checks and balances

More explicitly, it openly subscribes to the “unitary executive” theory advanced in Project 2025, which argues, in essence, that the president has total control over the executive branch, including agencies like the FBI and Justice Department that have traditionally exercised some independence.  Don’t believe me? Here’s Trump at a Turning Point conference in 2019: “Then I have an Article II, where I have the right to do whatever I want as president.” Or early in his second term: “ He who saves his Country does not violate any Law .” Stephen Miller said the quiet part out loud last year, too
In an interview on CNN’s News Central , he froze after asserting that the president has “ plenary authority ,” meaning Trump’s power is unreviewable and unquestioned

And here’s a line from Project 2025, which basically foretold our current constitutional crisis: The next Republican White House “must take seriously the duty to protect the powers and privileges of the President from encroachments by Congress, the judiciary, and the administrative components of departments and agencies.”  Is that how democracy works?  So what does that mean for the midterms? Of course, it’s tricky to be predictive
But when I hear Democrats say a new congressional majority will hold Trump accountable, I wonder if they should qualify those promises with a reality check
No blue wave can overcome the structural realities of gerrymandering, which has collapsed the number of competitive districts and disincentivized compromise

Cook Political Report found that mid-decade redistricting cut the number of competitive House seats from 87 to 77, meaning Democrats now need to win 57 of those 77 to take the chamber, up from 59 of 87 under the old lines
Cook projected Republicans gaining roughly eight seats from the redraws, Democrats two
Cook’s David Wasserman has noted that fewer than 5 percent of Americans are living in the districts that will truly decide House control
Control of the House is still up for grabs, but the narrower playing field makes sweeping change much harder
No wave can overcome conservative control of the courts, which has only grown in Trump’s second term
And most crucially, a wave matters less to a White House that thinks in such absolute terms, and sees Congress as something to be overcome, not worked with
In a typical administration, all the conditions for Trump’s last two years would point toward de-escalation
The public has fallen out of love with the administration’s priorities, he won’t be on the ballot in 2028, and Republicans would theoretically be freer to chart their own course
But as Trump has proven time and again, there’s no guarantee those rules apply to him, or to this version of the GOP
If anything, the 2024 presidential primary showed that Republicans are more likely to rally around Trump when they feel he’s being targeted by liberal Democrats

title: The surprisingly hopeful quest to fix concrete
excerpt: Concrete, one of the dirtiest substances ever concocted, could help save the planet | Aleksei Zotov/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images No, Rome was not
body: Concrete, one of the dirtiest substances ever concocted, could help save the planet | Aleksei Zotov/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images No, Rome was not built in a day, but it was built at breathtaking speed, its temples, amphitheaters, and aqueducts rising with the help of a magical blend of volcanic ash and lime

Today, that miraculous mortar has a less than enchanting name: concrete. “Romans lived through a true architectural revolution, and at the foundation of this revolution, literally, was a concrete discovery,” said Admir Masic, a materials science professor at MIT who made waves a few years ago for unearthing the fast-hardening secret sauce for why Roman concrete is so durable . “They were able to take a pile of dirt and mix it together, add water, and turn it into solid rock of any arbitrary size

It literally changed everything.” And yet, for a millennia after the fall of Rome, the world largely forgot about concrete, until, in the 18th century, an English mason found that mixing limestone and clay could form a paste that hardened underwater
Another few decades later, concrete as we now know it was reborn, and once again, it changed everything
In the centuries since, concrete has come to reshape our way of life, with disastrous results for the climate
What early concrete evangelists didn’t realize was that the modern way of producing the substance released giant amounts of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere
As it has become increasingly central to modernity, it has helped fuel environmental catastrophe
Today, however, a new generation of concretophiles like Masic have pored over the poured mixture in search of another miracle, a greener, more durable kind of concrete

And they’ve found multiple answers, from concrete that can heal its own cracks — as the Pantheon has for millennia — to electroconductive concrete capable of storing energy to a blend that allows concrete to soak up more CO2 than it emits.  Together, they suggest that in a not-so-distant future, concrete — yes, concrete — one of the dirtiest substances ever concocted, could help save the planet, transforming our built environment while actually intervening in the climate for the better.  How concrete built (and polluted) the modern world It’s no wonder that luminaries of the neo-concrete age, Thomas Edison among them, marveled at the stuff just as their Roman predecessors had

They saw it as a harbinger of utopia, of a world in which anything and everything — a home, an interstate highway, a water pipe, a subway system, or a grand piano — could be molded and poured for a fraction of ordinary costs.  “As to concrete dogs to stand warningly in the front yard and concrete cats to purr stonily under a concrete kitchen range,” the New York Times teased Edison in 1911 when he described his plans for a concrete home finished with concrete furnishings, “he made no announcement.” The beguiled inventor’s utopian vision of a world remade by concrete would come true in more ways than he realized
Muddy roads and rotting wooden sidewalks gave way to smooth gray pavement, and newly cast sewer systems saved millions of lives in the deathly dirty cities of the early industrial era

Concrete, when poured over rods of steel, proved strong enough to prop up colossal skyscrapers that Julius Caesar could only have dreamed of.  But there was a trade-off: Every time Edison fired up his trademark 150-foot kilns, scorching the limestone inside into blistering pebbles of cement clinker, he released hundreds of tons of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere

Yankee Stadium was built not by Babe Ruth’s swing alone, but with around 30,000 cubic yards of Edison concrete, whose creation released at least 5,400 tons of CO2, the equivalent of driving a gas-powered car 12.5 million miles, or to the moon and back more than two dozen times

But this is nothing compared with the roughly 30 billion tons of concrete the world now uses each year, enough to have turned the gluey gray goo into the second-most used material on Earth. (The first is water

Glug glug.) The Anthropocene has been built atop a foundation of concrete, its weight eclipsing the biomass of all living things, and its annual carbon tab responsible for up to 8 percent of global emissions , the equivalent of the entire country of India
Critically, unlike the astonishingly enduring remnants of Rome, our modern concrete decays quickly, so it must be repoured time and time again, which only makes it more environmentally catastrophic

But it doesn’t have to be this way, not anymore.  “The future of concrete is to think differently, to go away from claiming that cement is bad,” Masic told me. “Our goal is to turn this around and make concrete part of the solution instead of being a problem.” This is why we can have nice concrete Per ton, concrete actually emits far less CO2 by volume than other materials like aluminum, steel, plastic, or glass.  The problem is that we use so much of it, even a slightly negative footprint can quickly become enormous

But “the upside is,” said Sabbie Miller, a professor at UC Davis who focuses on sustainable concrete, “if you’re able to come up with some small change, then those small changes will also scale” in ways “that could have a huge effect on modern society and its burdens on the environment.”  One of those solutions takes a cue from the Romans, who made concrete differently than we do today

Their once-mysterious method ensured that hulking structures like the Colosseum or the Aqua Virgo, an aqueduct built during Augustus’ reign and still in use today, could survive for millennia while New York City’s Brooklyn-Queens Expressway or the Washington Bridge crumble after just a few decades of use
It’s not just that we drive cars over our concrete freeways while the Colosseum has been mostly free of even the bulkiest chariot wheels for millennia
The answer, according to Masic’s research, lies in the Romans’ ingenious recipe for cement, the glue that binds concrete together
When the ancients brewed a batch of cement, they left big white chunks of dormant lime in the final mixture
Later, if a crack formed, any water would react with the idle lime, filling the fissure with new stone

Our modern concrete has no such lime clasts, meaning that if water seeps into a crack, it degrades the structure from within, rusting the rebar that made our big towers possible, leading to a grim condition known as “ concrete cancer .”  Masic has recently turned his research into a startup called DMAT that reserves unreacted lime in concrete, giving it self-healing properties he says could extend a structure’s lifespan by about 50 percent, which in and of itself would reduce its carbon footprint by 40 percent

If the construction industry normalized such concrete or other mixtures that emit, say, half as much CO2 as usual, it would keep hundreds of millions of tons of it out of the atmosphere each year.  But why stop there? Some startups have gotten much better in recent years at producing concrete capable of quite literally breathing in more CO2 than it emits in a process that takes advantage of concrete’s natural porousness
It could, in theory, turn our cities into concrete rainforests by turning the material into a storage reservoir

As Miller put it, “what if we can use our concrete to undo some of our environmental damages that we’ve already caused?”  In the Bahamas, the startup Partanna has already built what it’s called the world’s first carbon net-negative home , an unassuming 1,250-square-foot abode that the company claims will sequester 182.6 tons of CO2 in its lifetime, the equivalent of hundreds of trees

Meanwhile, Masic’s lab has been piloting ways to turn concrete into a giant battery, capable of storing solar power during the day and releasing it at night, a green innovation that could cancel out its own carbon footprint within a few years of use.  Masic believes that electroconductivity could be key to catalyzing a new era of concrete — more so even than his neo-Roman ventures. “It might hold the secret,” he said, “for turning a bad guy into something amazing.” But as promising as these innovations are, it will take time for them to ripple out from model homes and into the concrete that actually surrounds us
American concrete startups have lost billions of dollars in federal funding and expected procurement contracts under the Trump administration
Some states, most notably California, are helping to pick up the slack, but investment still lags behind potential

There’s also the challenge of convincing builders running on paper thin margins that their old ways of doing things might fit better in a new mould.  But concrete’s staggering scale means that we can’t afford to keep pouring it without considering its ugly trade-offs
More importantly, perhaps, we can’t afford to miss out on the opportunity that such a mammoth, transformative material presents to change everything yet again.

title: The US military’s race to make fake blood
excerpt: Its call sign was Morphine 1-2.   In February 2007, the hulking dual-­rotor casualty evacuation helicopter had just flown three wounded soldiers to a field
body: Its call sign was Morphine 1-2.   In February 2007, the hulking dual-­rotor casualty evacuation helicopter had just flown three wounded soldiers to a field hospital in Balad, north of Baghdad, when another call came: an emergency mission to fly through an insurgent-controlled area in broad daylight

Typically, helicopters would be in a spot like this only at night, and with all lights turned off.  As it passed near the city of Karmah, in the eastern side of Al-Anbar province, an insurgent fired a portable missile launcher
The tail gunner, who likely saw the shot roaring in, yelled for the pilot to make an evasive move
But the missile had already locked on, and the ensuing blast started a fire on board
After the pilot battled the failing machine for 58 agonizing seconds, Morphine 1-2 plunged to the ground
All seven crew members were killed.   Why was the helo there in daylight? “It was getting blood and bringing it back

It was [on] what we call a ‘blood run,’ and [it’s] the highest of priorities besides casualty evacuation,” explains Lieutenant Commander Robert Murray, a Navy officer and program manager at DARPA, the Defense Advanced Research Projects Agency, who studied this incident as an intelligence officer
Today, a chronic shortage of blood in both the military and civilian worlds is fueling a race to develop synthetic alternatives
About 90% of preventable battlefield deaths are due to hemorrhage—bleeding that happens when a blood vessel ruptures—and it’s the leading cause of maternal deaths worldwide
A study published in Transfusion in 2025 found that of 1.2 million trauma patients in the United States who potentially needed blood before reaching a hospital, just 1% received it
The shortage results in about 10,000 preventable deaths each year in the US, according to the American College of Surgeons
Globally, that figure is likely in the millions .  One reason for the shortfall is that blood has a storage problem
Whole blood lasts only 35 days when refrigerated, so banks separate out components to stretch the timeline
The platelets that help wounds clot are typically stored at room temperature and last for a week or less
Hospitals and the military freeze the red blood cells that carry oxygen, as well as the protein-rich plasma that restores volume and aids coagulation

Once thawed, though, both will spoil within days. “What happens if I don’t know when I’m going to be attacked? Well, thaw it and you let it expire, right?” Murray says.  A JAMA study of combat injuries in Afghanistan suggests a magic number for someone who needs a transfusion: You have 36 minutes to get started
That’s why Murray—who, in addition to his military experience, has a PhD in physiology—is leading a DARPA effort to address blood’s battlefield problems
He’s in charge of a new $73 million dollar program called RAPIID (for “resuscitation and prevention of ischemia-induced dysfunction”)
Its goal is to create shelf-stable versions of the three major transfusion constituents: plasma, platelets, and red blood cells
As it gets underway late this year, RAPIID picks up on decades of work to synthesize blood or help it last longer

Most recently, that includes a prior $47.5 million DARPA project called FSHARP (for “fieldable solutions for hemorrhage with bio-artificial resuscitation products”), in which researchers have demonstrated promising results in animals.  KaloCyte techs use a device called a tangential flow filtration machine to process unencapsulated hemoglobin
MATT ROTH After processing, the hemoglobin is concentrated and then freeze-dried to make it shelf-stable
MATT ROTH With RAPIID trials for the different components occurring in parallel, the goal is to have bags of dried blood products deployed in the field by 2029

That puts Murray in the position of a conductor coordinating an orchestra of clinical trials with the FDA, while also sourcing the paraphernalia that goes along with transfusions—everything from combat-durable storage bags to tests that could check how much artificial blood a patient already has.  Getting it all done will be tough, but the military is feeling the pressure to address its shortage

Blood drives may not deliver in time after a mass-casualty event, and a JAMA study of combat injuries in Afghanistan suggests that if the injured person needs a transfusion, the magic number is 36 minutes. “If something is survivable—and generally we classify most all hemorrhage as survivable—[you’re] almost guaranteed to survive if you get the blood before that 36-minute mark,” Murray says
After that, the chance of survival “starts to drop precipitously.”   In the mission to make portable, shelf-stable blood components, plasma is the low-hanging fruit
Researchers have known how to isolate and freeze-dry plasma, the yellowish liquid that makes up 55% of whole human blood, since the late 1930s
On the battlefields of World War II, its mix of water, salts, and thousands of types of proteins helped restore blood volume in wounded soldiers—and to some degree controlled bleeding
In the 1960s, the US abandoned freeze-dried plasma because it carried a risk of transmitting hepatitis to recipients from infected donors
But screening, testing, and drying techniques improved, and starting in 2010, the US military launched a yearslong effort to rebuild its capacity for producing these products

Over the past two years, the FDA has allowed two types of freeze-dried plasma to be used in emergencies by the US military—and one can even be used by civilians.  As for platelets, efforts at extending their life date back to the 1950s, but they haven’t seen a ton of success
Bioengineers have, for example, attempted to attach the membranes of platelets to synthetic particles
The most successful project comes from a company called Cellphire, which freeze-dries actual human platelets
The product has shown safety and efficacy in humans in clinical trials, but its dependence on donors means it’s unclear whether this approach can scale
Red blood cells have been similarly tough to preserve or mimic
Their most critical component is hemoglobin, which carries oxygen and comes encased in a cell membrane

For more than a century, researchers have been looking for ways to deliver hemoglobin without the immunological challenges created by this exterior, including the fact that donors’ and recipients’ blood types need to be compatible
Evolutionary pressure developed that wrapper for very good reason, though: “Naked” hemoglobin tends to break down quickly in the bloodstream, and that can cause organ damage
It also scavenges nitric oxide, our body’s natural mechanism for opening up blood vessels, and causes those channels to constrict

This problem became all too clear in the 1980s and 1990s, when fears that transfusions could transmit HIV sparked interest in a class of membrane-free delivery mechanisms called hemoglobin-based oxygen carriers (HBOCs)

title: Trump is taking his midterms anger out on Ukraine
excerpt: Donald Trump walks to the White House from the South Lawn on October 10, 2026. | Alex Wroblewski/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff ,
body: Donald Trump walks to the White House from the South Lawn on October 10, 2026. | Alex Wroblewski/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: Is Trump turning on Ukraine?  What’s happening? Ukraine says its access to Starlink, the satellite internet system run by Elon Musk’s SpaceX company, and Starshield, the military version of the same technology, is being throttled as President Donald Trump’s animosity toward the country mounts

Why is Trump angry with Ukraine? Trump has been hot and cold on Ukraine since he returned to office, but his current anger is driven by oil prices and successful Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries — particularly ahead of the US midterm elections.  Last week, Trump announced a US-Russia diesel deal, which has elicited bipartisan anger and probably won’t do much , if anything, for diesel prices in the US
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has criticized the deal, leading Trump to lash out and call for Zelenskyy’s replacement

Over the weekend, Trump also announced an “ENERGY CEASEFIRE” between Ukraine and Russia that doesn’t really seem to exist . “Both parties have agreed,” he wrote. “Do not break it!” (Russia appears to have broken it the same day , while Ukraine is complying for now.) Is Ukraine actually to blame for high oil prices? Partially, but not primarily; as the BBC explains , while Ukrainian refinery strikes play a role, ongoing disruptions to the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf oil industry from Trump’s war with Iran have had a greater impact (though Trump has tried to shift the blame to Ukraine)
Why is Starlink so important? Starlink and Starshield provide vital communications infrastructure in Ukraine, especially on the battlefield
The technology is also used to control offensive and defensive Ukrainian drones, which have emerged as a key part of Ukraine’s military efforts against Russia

What’s next? Despite the fact that neither Russia nor Ukraine seemingly signed on to Trump’s “ENERGY CEASEFIRE” and Russia is still attacking Ukrainian energy facilities , Trump is trying to bind Ukraine to it: The US has reportedly threatened to suspend US intelligence sharing, which has helped give Ukraine early warning of Russian missile attacks, if Ukraine strikes more Russian refineries

And with that, it’s time to log off… I appreciated this New York Times story , pegged to Pope Leo XIV’s diagnosis yesterday, about all of the ways that science has made lung cancer massively more survivable than in years past, with a fatality rate half of what it was in the 1990s
Thanks for reading, have a great evening, and we’ll see you tomorrow!
